  • External ethics or compliance expert (independent perspective on conflict-of-interest, data integrity, and corporate governance)
  • Optional: external scientific integrity advisor (if clinical-study data management is novel or high-risk)

Decision Rights: Authority to develop and enforce compliance, ethics, and risk policies without Steering Committee approval (policies are informational unless they conflict with business decisions). Authority to audit and request corrections to regulatory submissions, marketing materials, and clinical-study documentation. Authority to escalate compliance violations, research misconduct, or unresolved conflicts of interest directly to CEO and investor board. Cannot unilaterally block a business decision (e.g., cannot stop a 510(k) submission), but can require documented risk disclosure to Steering Committee before decision is finalized.

Decision Mechanism: Consensus on policy development and risk assessment. Compliance violations are escalated by simple reporting (no vote needed). Risk escalation uses a quantitative risk-scoring matrix (likelihood 1-5 × severity 1-5 = 1-25 score); scores >9 are escalated immediately; scores 5-9 are tracked and reviewed quarterly. Data-integrity or research-misconduct allegations are investigated by the Chief Compliance Officer with external investigator involvement if needed; findings are reported to CEO and audit committee within 30 days.

Meeting Cadence: Quarterly compliance and risk reviews (2 hours); monthly check-ins with Quality/Regulatory on inspection readiness and design-control progress (1 hour); monthly data-integrity audits of clinical studies and analytical results (1 hour with academic partner); ad-hoc escalations (within 48 hours of identification).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Quarterly: regulatory roadmap status (FDA Pre-Sub prep, ISO 13485 timeline, CLIA application if applicable); inspection-readiness assessment; compliance violations or near-misses in past quarter; risk register review (technical, financial, regulatory, supply-chain, reputational risks); data-integrity audit findings; marketing/claims compliance check; conflict-of-interest disclosures and recusals
  • Monthly data-integrity: clinical-study enrollment and data-entry status; adverse-event reporting (if any); protocol deviations or amendments; data-audit findings; academic-partner communication and compliance
  • Monthly inspection-readiness: design-history-file completeness; change-control log review; training records and competency assessments; management-of-change documentation; complaint handling and adverse-event trending (if applicable)
  • Quarterly risk register: update likelihood and severity for all identified risks; identify new risks; track mitigation-plan progress; escalate scores >9; discuss risk interdependencies (e.g., plasma-separation failure cascades to all clusters)

Escalation Path: Compliance violations (regulatory breach, research misconduct allegation, conflict-of-interest violation) escalate to CEO and board audit committee within 48 hours. Risk scores >9 (e.g., combined technical + financial risk of design failure + funding gap) escalate to Steering Committee within 5 business days with mitigation options. Data-integrity concerns (suspected selective reporting, falsification) trigger independent investigation and escalation to CEO and board within 30 days. Marketing or claims non-compliance (use of '500 tests' claim before validation) is escalated to CEO and chief marketing officer within 24 hours.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor (or CEO/Founder acting as initiating authority) in coordination with Lead Investor

  • Steering Committee membership roster with names, titles, affiliations
  • Signed commitment letters from all 5 members confirming availability
  • Conflict-of-interest disclosure forms (signed by each member)

  • CEO/Founder, CFO, R&D and Quality leadership roles defined and staffing authorized

Project Steering Committee hold inaugural founding meeting (2-3 hours) to finalize charter, define Fallback Panel V1 (50-analyte core with 4-5 cartridges), lock gate criteria (yield ≥85%, concordance ≥95%, shelf-life ≥12 months, plasma separation ≥95%, COGS ≤USD 25/cartridge), approve capital tranches and timeline, assign gate-meeting chair (typically CEO), establish monthly dashboard and reporting cadence.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Steering Committee (newly formed)

10. Responsible Body/Role: Chief Quality Officer / Regulatory Lead (lead) with regulatory consultant and Chief R&D Officer

Suggested Timeframe: FDA review Months 30-48 (2029-04-13 to 2030-10-13); decision expected Months 36-48 (2029-10-13 to 2030-10-13)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • FDA Submission Acknowledgment and Review Clock Start (received Month 30 = 2029-04-13)
  • FDA Deficiency Letter or Q-Submission Requests (if any, expected Month 36-42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13)
  • Responses to FDA Deficiencies (prepared and submitted within 30-60 days of FDA request)
  • FDA Clearance/Approval Letter (received Months 36-48 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-10-13)

Dependencies:

  • 510(k) or De Novo submission filed Month 30 (2029-04-13)
  • Quality system and design controls mature (ISO 13485 certified by Month 18 = 2028-04-13)

62. Operations Committee prepare post-clearance commercial launch plan. Define: manufacturing scale-up (ramp from 10k to 50k cartridges/month over Months 48-72 = 2030-10-13 to 2032-10-13), sales-channel activation (direct to reference labs, point-of-care clinics, or pharmacy partnerships), clinical-site and payer onboarding, training for operators and support staff, cold-chain logistics setup, and customer-support infrastructure. Target commercial launch by Month 48 (2030-10-13).

Responsible Body/Role: Operations Committee (Chief R&D Officer, Manufacturing Lead, Chief Quality Officer) with Commercial/Sales Lead

Suggested Timeframe: Months 36-48 (2029-10-13 to 2030-10-13) for launch-plan finalization

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Post-Clearance Commercial Launch Plan (manufacturing scale-up, sales channels, training, support, timeline)
  • First Commercial Cartridge Shipment Plan (date, volume, customer sites, fulfillment logistics)

Dependencies:

  • FDA clearance received (expected Months 36-48 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-10-13)
  • Manufacturing scale-up validation complete (by Month 30 = 2029-04-13)

63. Project Steering Committee oversee Cluster 1 commercial launch and Cluster 2 development initiation (Months 48-72 = 2030-10-13 to 2032-10-13). Monitor: first-year revenue, operational yield and quality metrics, payer-coverage uptake, clinical adoption, and regulatory/pharmacovigilance performance. Manage Cluster 2 development timeline and gate-linked capital releases. Track expansion toward the 500-analyte cumulative menu (estimated 10 clusters of 50 analytes each, which would require Months 48-120 = 2030-10-13 to 2036-10-13 if clusters clear sequentially at 6-9 months post-launch). Communicate progress and re-planning to investors.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Steering Committee (CEO, Lead Investor, CFO, Chief R&D Officer, Chief Quality Officer) with Commercial/Operations team

Suggested Timeframe: Months 48-72 (2030-10-13 to 2032-10-13) and beyond for ongoing governance

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Monthly Commercial Operations Reports (revenue, units shipped, yield, quality metrics, customer feedback, adoption trends)
  • Cluster 2 Development Progress Reports (analyte selection, clinical study planning, regulatory strategy, funding status)
  • Expansion Roadmap Updates (revised timelines for Clusters 3-10, adjusted for market demand and technical learnings)

Dependencies:

  • Cluster 1 FDA clearance and commercial launch complete (Month 48 = 2030-10-13)
  • Series B and Series C/D funding in place for Cluster 2+ development

Decision Escalation Matrix

Budget or Capital Expenditure Exceeding Project Steering Committee Authorization Limit Escalation Level: Investor Board or Lead Investor Approval Process: Lead Investor reviews the capital request, convenes board vote if required by equity agreements, and approves or denies capital tranche release. Decision documented in board minutes with financial justification and impact on timeline/scope. Rationale: Gate-linked capital tranches (Seed, Series A Tranches 1-3, Series B, Series C) require board-level approval to release funds beyond Operations Committee authority (USD 500k ceiling). Unbudgeted capital requests (e.g., emergency supplier surcharge, equipment overrun >20%, unexpected regulatory consulting) that exceed monthly gate-allocated burn require investor approval to preserve cash discipline and avoid uncontrolled spend. Negative Consequences: Uncontrolled capital spend beyond gate budgets consumes runway prematurely, forces unplanned fundraising rounds at adverse valuation, delays development by 2-4 months due to funding gaps, or triggers forced lean pivot earlier than planned, stranding previous investments and demoralizing the team.

Technical Gate Failure or Ambiguous Gate Results Requiring Fallback Panel V1 Retreat Decision Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee with Technical Advisory Group Assessment Approval Process: Operations Committee prepares gate data (yield, concordance, CV, shelf-life). Technical Advisory Group validates results within 3 business days. Steering Committee holds emergency gate-review meeting (within 1 week of gate miss) and votes on: (1) retest/redesign plan with 4-week extension, or (2) activate Fallback Panel V1 (50 analytes, immediate). Board approval required if retreat impacts Series A/B commitments or extends timeline >6 months. Rationale: Analytical-feasibility gates (plasma separation ≥95% at Month 6 = 2027-04-13; yield ≥85% at Month 12 = 2027-10-13; shelf-life ≥12 months projected; concordance ≥95%) are the primary technical checkpoints. A miss (yield 80-85%, shelf-life 8-11 months, concordance 93-95%) triggers ambiguity requiring Technical Advisory Group validation and Steering Committee judgment on pursue-vs-retreat. Fallback V1 retreat is a strategic decision affecting product scope, revenue potential, and funder expectations. Negative Consequences: Delayed or absent gate decision creates sunk-cost escalation: unrealistic hope prolongs spending on unviable design, consumes USD 3-10M in unrecovered capital, extends pre-revenue runway to Months 54-72 (2031-04-13 to 2032-10-13), and may result in product with insufficient market validation or manufacturability, causing late-stage failure at Months 36-48 (2029-10-13 to 2030-10-13) pre-approval inspection.

Scope Retreat Decision: Fallback Panel V1 Analyte Removal or Menu Narrowing Below 50 Analytes Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee with Chief Compliance Officer and CEO to Investor Board Approval Process: Chief Compliance Officer / Regulatory Lead documents FDA feedback (Pre-Submission response, Q-Submission answer, or deficiency letter). Operations Committee and Technical Advisory Group assess impact on design, clinical study, and timeline. Steering Committee votes on response (e.g., additional clinical sites, expanded sample size, new biocompatibility testing, shelf-life retest). If impact exceeds USD 2M or 6 months, escalate to investor board with two options: (1) absorb cost and timeline, or (2) narrow Fallback V1 scope to accelerate path. Rationale: FDA pathway (510(k) vs. De Novo) determines evidence burden and timeline. Pre-Submission feedback is advisory; FDA may later require different evidence in actual submission. De Novo requirement (instead of 510(k)) adds 12-18 months and USD 2-4M. Major protocol amendment (e.g., FDA requests outcomes study vs. method-comparison) extends clinical timeline by 6-12 months. These changes cascade to funding need, investor expectations, and competitive positioning, requiring top-level decision. Negative Consequences: Unaddressed regulatory-pathway uncertainty results in developing wrong evidence package, forcing redesign or re-study at Months 30-36 (2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13), adding 6-18 months and USD 2-4M to clearance timeline. If discovery occurs post-Phase 1 submission (Month 30 = 2029-04-13), FDA deficiency response adds 3-6 months. Investor funding gap widens by USD 5-15M; Series B/C timing slips; competitive entry risk increases.

Design Change, Analyte Removal, or Product-Scope Modification Affecting Fallback Panel V1 Definition or Cluster Roadmap Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee (if ≥10% of Fallback V1 affected or >USD 500k cost); Investor Board (if >25% of menu affected or strategic retreat) Approval Process: Operations Committee documents the design change, analyte failure, or scope request. Technical Advisory Group assesses feasibility impact. If change is <USD 50k and <2 weeks timeline, Operations Committee approves and reports to Steering Committee monthly. If change ≥USD 50k or ≥2 weeks impact, Steering Committee votes within 1 week. If ≥10% of Fallback V1 or ambiguous clinical impact, Steering Committee escalates to investor board with risk assessment and revised product definition. Rationale: Fallback Panel V1 is the guaranteed product and funder commitment. Removing analytes or narrowing menu scope changes product differentiation, revenue potential, and investor return. Design changes after Month 6 (2027-04-13) lock in cost and manufacturing decisions; changes to fluidic geometry, reagent volumes, or cartridge footprint after mold ordering (expected Month 6-9 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-07-13) trigger re-tooling cost (USD 50-150k, 3-4 months). Scope creep (adding analytes) delays design freeze and manufacturing readiness. Negative Consequences: Uncontrolled design changes delay design freeze from Month 18 (2028-04-13) to Month 24-30 (2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13), pushing clinical study and FDA submission 6-12 months. Re-tooling molds and equipment adds USD 50-200k and 4-8 weeks. Product scope uncertainty erodes investor confidence in Series B/C fundraising. Analyte removals (e.g., due to cross-reactivity or sensitivity failure) not escalated to Steering Committee can silently degrade product and credibility (e.g., delivering 35-analyte menu instead of 50, surprising customers post-launch).

Funding Gap, Unexpected Burn, or Pharma Revenue Shortfall Threatening Runway Beyond 6 Months Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee to Investor Board and CEO Approval Process: CFO / Finance Lead reports monthly cash burn vs. budget and forecasts runway. If variance exceeds 10% of monthly burn or cumulative gap >6 months of operations, Steering Committee is notified within 1 week. If gap cannot be closed by spending cuts or pharma acceleration, CEO and Steering Committee convene emergency board meeting (within 2 weeks) to approve contingency: (1) lean-pivot activation (20-30% headcount reduction, pause Newark Phase 2, focus on CLIA fallback or narrow beachhead), (2) bridge financing (debt or down-round equity), or (3) partnership/acquisition discussions. Rationale: Pharma revenue is contingent on sponsor commitments and is inherently uncertain. Non-dilutive funding (grants) is variable and timing-dependent. Equipment lead times and cost overruns are common. Funding gaps at Months 12-18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) or Months 24-30 (2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13) are high-probability risks given the lean-pivot trigger (pharma <USD 100k/month at Month 18 = 2028-04-13). Early warning and board-level escalation preserves optionality (lean pivot, partnership) vs. forced crisis-mode decisions. Negative Consequences: Funding shortfall discovered at Month 18 (2028-04-13) with only 2-3 months runway forces emergency bridge financing at 40-60% valuation discount, diluting Series A and founder shares by 10-20%. Missed payroll or unplanned headcount cuts destabilize team and cause key-person departures (2-3 month productivity loss). Delayed Newark Phase 2 equipment orders miss 6-month lead times, pushing manufacturing readiness to Months 30-36 (2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13) and FDA submission to Months 36-42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13), compressing pre-clearance window and increasing competitive risk.

Critical Supplier Failure, Quality Defect, or Single-Source Dependency Crisis (Defect Rate >10% or Delivery Failure >2 Weeks) Escalation Level: Operations Committee to Project Steering Committee (if duration >4 weeks or recovery cost >USD 100k) Approval Process: Procurement Lead and Quality Scorecard Owner flag supplier defect rate >10% or delivery delay >2 weeks within 1 week of discovery. Operations Committee votes to activate backup supplier (within 2-week window if pre-qualified). If backup activation costs >USD 100k, requires USD 500k+ authority check-in with Steering Committee within 5 business days. If supplier failure affects clinical-study or FDA-submission timeline by >2 weeks, escalate to Steering Committee for risk mitigation approval (expedited re-qualification, alternative material sourcing, design pivot). Rationale: Contract molders, reagent suppliers, and logistics partners are external dependencies. Yield loss due to molder defects, reagent lot failures due to supplier quality drift, and logistics delays all directly impact cartridge availability, clinical-study enrollment, and regulatory-submission timeline. Single-source suppliers (identified during supply-chain risk assessment at Month 4 = 2027-02-13) without dual-source qualification expose the program to 4-8 week production halts if primary supplier fails. Negative Consequences: Unaddressed supplier defect discovered at Month 12-15 (2027-10-13 to 2028-01-13) during pilot fills delays cartridge availability for clinical study by 4-8 weeks, compressing enrollment window from 6 to 2-3 months and reducing statistical power. Reagent supplier discontinuation or price shock at Months 18-24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13) forces re-qualification of alternative supplier (4-8 weeks) and potential re-validation of assay (USD 100-300k, 4-8 weeks), pushing clinical-study close-out to Month 30 (2029-04-13) and FDA submission to Months 36-42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13). Logistics failure (cold-chain outage) during clinical distribution spoils cartridge lots (USD 50-150k loss, 2-4 week replacement delay).

Reputational or Compliance Risk: Over-Claiming, Data Integrity Violation, Conflict-of-Interest Disclosure, or Regulatory Non-Compliance Discovery Escalation Level: Chief Compliance Officer and Compliance, Ethics and Risk Management Committee to Investor Board and Legal Counsel Approval Process: Chief Compliance Officer investigates allegation within 48 hours. If substantiated (e.g., '500 tests per drop' claim made prematurely, analyte data selectively excluded from Analyte Performance Report, conflict of interest undisclosed), compliance committee convenes within 1 week. Response options: (1) public corrective statement and remediation plan, (2) internal investigation and disciplinary action, (3) notification to FDA or relevant regulator, (4) legal review and liability assessment. Board is notified immediately if issue impacts regulatory submissions, investor communications, or company valuation >5%. Rationale: Diagnostics industry credibility is built on transparent, accurate data and regulatory compliance. Historical context of failed single-drop claims creates reputational vulnerability. Over-claiming (e.g., 500 tests before validation), selective data reporting (publishing only passing analytes, hiding failures), or regulatory breaches (false statements in FDA submissions) are high-severity risks with potential FDA enforcement (warning letter, import detention, criminal referral) and investor confidence loss. Undisclosed conflicts of interest (e.g., board member has equity in supplier) create legal liability. Negative Consequences: Discovered over-claim at Month 12-18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) results in corrective media statement, Series A/B fundraising delay or valuation haircut 20-50%, FDA warning letter or submission rejection adding 6-12 months and USD 2-4M to remediation. Data-integrity violation (e.g., analyte failure data omitted from FDA submission) discovered at pre-approval inspection triggers 483 observations, delays clearance 3-6 months, and exposes company to FDA enforcement action or OIG investigation. Undisclosed conflict of interest triggers board-level restructuring and potential fiduciary-duty litigation against founders/early investors.

Monitoring Progress

1. Analytical Feasibility and Assay Performance Tracking (Gate Criteria Monitoring)

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Analyte Performance Report (monthly spreadsheet/dashboard: concordance, CV, shelf-life projection, yield, status per analyte)
  • Analyte Review Meeting Minutes (monthly assessment of pass/fail/redesign/retire decisions)
  • Cross-Reactivity Screening Data (Month 4-6 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-04-13 experimental results)
  • Pilot Yield and Lot-Consistency Records (first-article run Month 12 = 2027-10-13 data)
  • Stability Testing Database (real-time and accelerated-stability results, Arrhenius projections)

Frequency: Monthly Analyte Review Meetings (Months 3-12 = 2027-01-13 to 2027-10-13, then quarterly). Formal gate assessments at Months 6, 12, 18 (2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13). Technical Advisory Group validation of gate results within 3 business days before Steering Committee vote.

Responsible Role: Operations Committee (Chief R&D Officer, Assay Chemistry Lead, Chief Quality Officer) owns monthly tracking. Technical Advisory Group (external microfluidics, immunoassay, manufacturing experts) validates analytical feasibility and manufacturing-yield assessments. Steering Committee votes on gate passage.

Adaptation Process: Monthly Analyte Review identifies analyte failures (concordance <95%, CV >10%, shelf-life <9 months projected). Decision logic: if threshold miss, Operations Committee decides within 2 weeks whether to (a) redesign and retest within 4-8 weeks, (b) retire analyte from panel and update Fallback Panel V1 roster, or (c) defer to Cluster 2. Retired analytes are documented in Analyte Performance Report with root-cause analysis, visible to board and FDA. If ≥10% of Cluster 1 analytes require retirement or major redesign, escalate to Steering Committee for scope impact and gate-delay assessment. Formal gate failures (e.g., pilot yield <80% at Month 12 = 2027-10-13) trigger 4-week design-review cycle; if unresolved by Month 15 (2028-01-13), Steering Committee votes to activate Fallback Panel V1 (50-analyte core) or pursue extended redesign with capital reallocation.

Adaptation Trigger: Month 6 (2027-04-13) gate: plasma separation ≥95% yield from ≥100 fingerstick subjects with ≥1.6 µL usable plasma, hemolysis index <50; cross-reactivity ≤5% bias at 10× interferent; COGS ceiling USD 25/cartridge locked (proposed threshold). Month 12 (2027-10-13) analytical feasibility gate: pilot-scale yield ≥85% (mean, lower 95% CI ≥80%), lot-to-lot CV <10%, shelf-life ≥12 months projected (Arrhenius R² >0.90), analytical concordance ≥95% from preliminary clinical data (100-150 samples); modeled COGS ≤USD 25 (proposed threshold). Month 18 (2028-04-13) design-freeze gate: lead-cluster design locked, interim clinical concordance ≥95% (lower CI ≥93%, 150-200 enrolled subjects), Newark pilot fills yield ≥85%, ISO 13485 certified (proposed threshold). Any analyte failing monthly thresholds for 2+ months → retire/redesign decision. Yield or concordance miss at gate → retest plan (2-3 week escalation) or Fallback V1 retreat (Steering Committee vote).

2. Capital Tranche Release and Budget Variance Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • 60-Month Cash-Flow Model (Months 0-60 = 2026-10-13 to 2031-10-13 with quarterly burn rates and gate-linked tranche schedule)
  • Monthly Cash Burn Report (actual spend vs. budgeted by project phase: R&D, Newark, clinical, regulatory, G&A)
  • Pharma Contract and Grant Revenue Tracking (signed contracts, revenue received, pipeline status)
  • Capital Tranche Release Log (Seed, Series A Tranches 1-3, Series B; dates, amounts, gate thresholds, board approvals)

Frequency: Monthly cash-burn tracking and variance reporting (actuals vs. forecast ±10% variance flag). Gate-linked capital releases voted at Months 6, 12, 18, 24 (2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-10-13). Emergency Steering Committee meeting within 1 week if cumulative variance >10% monthly burn or runway gap >6 months.

Responsible Role: CFO / Finance Lead owns monthly cash-flow reporting and variance analysis. Steering Committee approves each capital-tranche release before funds are drawn (pass/fail/defer vote tied to gate criteria). If funding gap emerges >6 months, CEO escalates to investor board for lean-pivot approval or bridge-financing decision within 2 weeks.

Adaptation Process: Monthly cash-burn report compared to gate-linked budget (Seed USD 2-3M Months 0-6 = 2026-10-13 to 2027-04-13; Series A Tranche 1 USD 3-4M at Month 6 = 2027-04-13 gate; etc.). If actuals exceed monthly budget by >15%, Finance Lead investigates variance and proposes corrective action (spending cuts, project re-scoping, accelerated revenue) to Steering Committee within 5 business days. If cumulative variance indicates cash runway <6 months, CFO convenes emergency Steering Committee within 1 week. Options voted: (a) accelerate fundraising (bridge round, Series B pull-forward), (b) activate lean-pivot contingency (20-30% headcount reduction, pause Newark Phase 2, refocus on CLIA or narrow beachhead), or (c) seek strategic partnership/acquisition. Pharma-revenue shortfall (cumulative <USD 500k by Month 18 = 2028-04-13, or run-rate <USD 100k/month by Month 18 = 2028-04-13) automatically triggers lean-pivot review within 2 weeks per pre-agreed threshold.

Adaptation Trigger: Cumulative burn exceeds gate-linked budget by >15% (or USD 500k cumulative variance) for any month. Pharma/grant revenue below USD 1-2M cumulative target by Month 12 (2027-10-13), or <USD 100k/month run-rate at Month 18 (2028-04-13) → lean-pivot eligible (proposed threshold). Runway forecast <6 months at any month → emergency funding decision required (Steering Committee escalation, investor board vote within 2 weeks). Series A or B tranche gate fails (e.g., Month 12 = 2027-10-13 analytical feasibility not met) → capital release is withheld; Operations Committee has 4 weeks to retest/redesign, or Fallback V1 is activated and capital is reallocated to narrower scope.

3. Regulatory Pathway Alignment and FDA Pre-Submission Feedback Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • FDA Pre-Submission Meeting Minutes and Agency Feedback Summary (Month 6 = 2027-04-13 expected)
  • Regulatory Roadmap Document (510(k) vs. De Novo assessment, evidence requirements, submission timeline)
  • ISO 13485 and Design-Control Compliance Checklist (design controls, DHF completeness, management of change, supplier agreements, training records)
  • Quality-System Audit Reports (internal ISO 13485 assessment Month 15 = 2028-01-13, certification audit Month 18 = 2028-04-13)
  • IEC 62304 Software Development Lifecycle Documentation (requirements, design, testing, version control)

Frequency: Pre-Submission meeting held Month 6 (2027-04-13); FDA feedback documented and disseminated within 2 weeks. ISO 13485 compliance assessed at Month 15 (2028-01-13); formal certification audit Month 18 (2028-04-13); ongoing compliance audits quarterly thereafter. Mock FDA pre-approval inspection Months 28-30 (2029-02-13 to 2029-04-13). Regulatory roadmap reviewed and confirmed by Steering Committee at Months 12, 18 (2027-10-13, 2028-04-13).

Responsible Role: Chief Quality Officer / Regulatory Lead owns regulatory-pathway strategy and quality-system readiness. Chief Compliance Officer oversees Pre-Submission preparation and FDA communication. External regulatory consultant (retained Months 0-6 = 2026-10-13 to 2027-04-13, budget USD 50-100k) supports Pre-Sub meeting and submission package preparation. Technical Advisory Group reviews regulatory evidence adequacy (study design, sample-size calculations, analytical acceptance criteria) at Month 18 (2028-04-13).

Adaptation Process: FDA Pre-Submission feedback (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) is reviewed by Steering Committee within 1 week; if pathway changes from 510(k) expected to De Novo likely (adding 12-18 months and USD 2-4M), Steering Committee votes on: (a) proceed with De Novo evidence package and extend funding model, or (b) narrow product scope to de-risk De Novo or pursue Fallback V1 + CLIA lab-service route. If FDA indicates additional clinical or analytical evidence needed, Operations Committee assesses impact on clinical-study protocol, timeline, and cost; if impact >USD 2M or >6 months, escalate to Steering Committee and investor board for funding/scope decision. ISO 13485 compliance gaps identified at Month 15 (2028-01-13) assessment are incorporated into corrective-action plan due by Month 18 (2028-04-13); if major gaps remain unclosed (design-control deficiency, supplier-agreement gaps, complaint-handling procedures), design freeze is delayed and Steering Committee is notified of inspection-readiness risk. Mock FDA inspection (Months 28-30 = 2029-02-13 to 2029-04-13) findings are tracked; 483-level observations must be closed within 2-4 weeks before real pre-approval inspection. Any FDA Q-Submission or deficiency letter post-submission (expected Months 36-42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13) is escalated to Steering Committee within 3 business days with recommended response and timeline.

Adaptation Trigger: FDA Pre-Submission feedback indicates De Novo pathway is likely (vs. 510(k) assumed) → Steering Committee decision within 1 week: continue De Novo (budget/timeline impact = +12-18 months, +USD 2-4M) or pivot to narrower scope/fallback. Major regulatory evidence gap identified (e.g., FDA requires outcomes study or expanded sample size) → impact assessment and Steering Committee decision on cost/timeline trade-off within 2 weeks. ISO 13485 assessment reveals major non-conformance (design-control deficiency) → corrective-action plan required, design freeze delayed if not resolved by Month 18 (2028-04-13). Mock FDA inspection identifies ≥5 potential 483-level observations → remediation plan developed and closed within 4 weeks, or pre-approval inspection delayed by 2-4 months. Any FDA Q-Submission deficiency or major comments post-submission (Month 36-42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13) → response prepared within 30-60 days per FDA timeline; if deficiency indicates fundamental design or evidence issue, escalate to Steering Committee with re-design/re-test scope and cost.

4. Pharma Beachhead Revenue and Commercial-Validation Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Pharma Partnership Pipeline Tracker (5-10 prospects, status: interest, negotiation, signed contract, data-generation in progress, results received)
  • Signed Pharma Contracts Register (2-3 contracts expected by Month 9 = 2027-07-13; terms: sample volume, pricing, timeline, data ownership)
  • Monthly Pharma Revenue Report (cumulative and run-rate USD, invoiced and received, collection status)
  • Non-Dilutive Funding Pipeline (SBIR/STTR grant applications, expected award dates, amounts received)
  • Lean-Pivot Trigger Checklist (cumulative revenue <USD 500k by Month 12 = 2027-10-13 or run-rate <USD 100k/month by Month 18 = 2028-04-13)

Frequency: Monthly pharma-partnership status calls with key sponsors (Months 3-18 = 2027-01-13 to 2028-04-13). Revenue reporting monthly (actual invoices and collections). Quarterly pharma/grant pipeline review with Steering Committee (Months 6, 12, 18, 24 = 2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-10-13). Lean-pivot trigger assessed at Month 18 (2028-04-13); decision made within 2 weeks if triggered.

Responsible Role: CEO / Founder (business development lead) owns pharma relationship and sponsorship strategy. Finance Lead tracks revenue received and burn-rate impact. Steering Committee reviews pharma pipeline quarterly and votes on lean-pivot activation if trigger is met.

Adaptation Process: Monthly pharma calls track: (1) feasibility-phase partnership status (Months 3-6 = 2027-01-13 to 2027-04-13, no funding expected), (2) contract-negotiation status (Months 6-9 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-07-13, first contract signatures targeted), (3) data-generation in progress (Months 9-18 = 2027-07-13 to 2028-04-13, samples processed, results reporting). If pharma partner delays signing or reduces sample volume >30%, CEO escalates to Steering Committee and re-evaluates revenue forecast. If cumulative pharma revenue is <USD 100k by Month 12 (2027-10-13), or projected run-rate at Month 18 (2028-04-13) is <USD 100k/month, Steering Committee convenes within 1 week and votes on lean-pivot contingency: (a) reduce headcount 20-30% (preserve R&D, quality, clinical readiness; defer Clusters 2-5), (b) pause Newark Phase 2 equipment orders (continue only Phase 1 reagent lab), (c) accelerate CLIA lab-service fallback preparation (Month 12 = 2027-10-13 target), (d) pursue alternative funding (bridge, Series B pull-forward, partnership). Non-dilutive funding (SBIR/STTR) applications submitted by Month 4-5 (2027-02-13 to 2027-03-13); Phase 1 awards (USD 100-500k) expected Month 10-12 (2027-08-13 to 2027-10-13). If SBIR/STTR awards are delayed or rejected, fundraising target (Series A sizing) is re-evaluated.

Adaptation Trigger: Cumulative pharma contract revenue <USD 500k by Month 12 (2027-10-13) (proposed threshold) → reassess revenue strategy; if <USD 1M cumulative by Month 18 (2028-04-13), lean-pivot contingency is activated. Pharma partner contract negotiations slip >4 months past target (e.g., expected signature Month 9 = 2027-07-13 delays to Month 13 = 2027-11-13) → CEO and Steering Committee re-plan cash burn and fundraising timeline within 2 weeks. First pharma contract not signed by Month 9 (2027-07-13) → Series A Tranche 1 funding (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) contingency reassessed; if pharma deal remains unsigned by Month 12 (2027-10-13), lean-pivot triggered automatically. Run-rate below USD 100k/month at Month 18 (2028-04-13) assessment → lean-pivot contingency activated within 2 weeks (proposed threshold). Non-dilutive funding awards fall short of USD 1-2M target by >30% (e.g., only USD 500k of USD 1.5M applied) → Series A/B sizing increased to compensate, or spending reduced accordingly.

5. Newark Manufacturing Build-Out and Capital-Committed Assurance Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Newark Facility Lease Agreement and Site-Selection Documentation (by Month 14 = 2027-12-13, contingent on Month 12 = 2027-10-13 gate)
  • Phase 1 Equipment Procurement List and Quotes (reagent hood, refrigerated storage, QC instruments; ordered Months 4-6 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-04-13, lead times 4-6 months)
  • Phase 1 Fit-Out Timeline and Budget (Months 12-15 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-01-13, capital USD 500-800k; operational by Month 15-18 = 2028-01-13 to 2028-04-13)
  • Pilot-Fill Results and Yield Validation Records (Month 12-18 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13 batches, yield ≥85% target)
  • Phase 2 Equipment Procurement Plan and Long-Lead Orders (Months 18-24 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13, capital USD 2-4M + 20% contingency USD 400-600k, operational by Months 24-30 = 2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13)

Frequency: Monthly Newark facility and equipment status (fit-out progress, equipment deliveries, installation schedule, pilot fills). Gate-linked capital release votes at Months 12, 18 (2027-10-13, 2028-04-13): Phase 1 capital USD 500-800k approved at Month 12 (2027-10-13) gate (after analytical feasibility pass); Phase 2 capital USD 2-4M approved at Month 18 (2028-04-13) gate (after design freeze and pilot yield ≥85%).

Responsible Role: Operations Committee (Manufacturing Lead, Chief Quality Officer) owns Newark facility planning and equipment procurement. CFO / Finance Lead manages capital budgets and equipment ordering authority. Steering Committee votes on capital release for each phase before commitment is made.

Adaptation Process: Month 12 (2027-10-13) gate: if analytical feasibility passes (yield, concordance, shelf-life thresholds met), Steering Committee approves Phase 1 capital release (USD 500-800k) and authorizes Newark site selection and lease negotiation. If gate fails, Phase 1 is paused (no facility lease, no equipment orders). Phase 1 fit-out (Months 12-15 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-01-13) is tracked monthly: equipment delivery dates, installation progress, pilot-fill scheduling. If pilot-fill yield from Phase 1 is <85% (lower 95% CI <80%), design-review cycle is triggered; Phase 2 commitment is deferred until redesign is resolved and retest yield is ≥85%. If Phase 1 equipment costs exceed quoted price by >20% or lead times slip >4 weeks, Finance Lead escalates to Steering Committee within 1 week for contingency-fund approval (20% contingency reserve is pre-allocated for such overruns). Month 18 (2028-04-13) gate: if design freeze and yield validation are confirmed, Phase 2 capital release (USD 2-4M) is approved. Long-lead equipment (automated cartridge filler, 6-12 month lead time) is ordered immediately upon approval; binding orders with non-cancellable deposits are placed. Phase 2 fit-out (Months 18-30 = 2028-04-13 to 2029-04-13) is tracked monthly; equipment commissioning and scale-up validation are completed by Month 30 (2029-04-13) to support manufacturing readiness for FDA pre-approval inspection (expected Months 36-42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13).

Adaptation Trigger: Month 12 (2027-10-13) analytical feasibility gate fails (yield <80%, concordance <95%, shelf-life <9 months) → Phase 1 commitment is paused; no facility lease signed, no equipment orders placed. Steering Committee decides within 2 weeks: (a) retest and redesign (extend by 4-8 weeks), (b) activate Fallback V1 and cancel Newark Phase 1 (pivot to contract-manufacturer and CLIA lab-service fallback). Phase 1 pilot-fill yield <85% at Month 12-15 (2027-10-13 to 2028-01-13) → design-review cycle triggered; Phase 2 approval delayed until yield is restored to ≥85% via redesign (additional 4-8 weeks, +USD 100-300k). Phase 1 or Phase 2 equipment costs exceed budget by >20% (each phase) → 20% contingency is applied; if contingency is exhausted, Steering Committee votes on additional capital request or spending cuts elsewhere. Long-lead equipment delivery slip >6 weeks (e.g., filling machine delivery delays from Month 24 = 2028-10-13 to Month 30 = 2029-04-13) → alternative equipment sourcing or contract-manufacturer contingency activated within 2 weeks; manufacturing scale-up readiness by Month 30 (2029-04-13) may be at risk, escalating FDA pre-approval inspection readiness.

6. Clinical Study Enrollment and Data Integrity Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Clinical-Study Protocol and IRB Approval Documentation (by Month 12 = 2027-10-13)
  • Subject-Enrollment Tracking Dashboard (monthly: target vs. actual, sites activated, protocol-deviation rate, adverse events)
  • LIMS Integration and eCRF System (data entry, quality checks, result reporting to device and reference lab)
  • Clinical-Study Data-Integrity Audit Reports (quarterly data audits of measurement accuracy, traceability, adverse-event reporting)
  • Interim Clinical-Data Analysis Report (Months 18, 24 = 2028-04-13, 2028-10-13: concordance, CV, sensitivity/specificity per analyte)

Frequency: Monthly clinical-study enrollment tracking (vs. target 300-500 subjects over Months 12-18 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13). Data-integrity audits quarterly (Months 15, 18, 21, 24 = 2028-01-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-07-13, 2028-10-13). Interim concordance analysis at Months 18, 24 (2028-04-13, 2028-10-13) from 100-150 and 200+ subjects respectively. Final analysis and publication target Month 30 (2029-04-13).

Responsible Role: Chief Compliance Officer / Regulatory Lead (study governance, protocol adherence, data integrity). Clinical-Trial Coordinator (day-to-day enrollment, site coordination, informed consent, adverse-event reporting). Academic clinical partner (site activation, subject recruitment, sample collection, reference-lab testing). Compliance, Ethics and Risk Management Committee (data-integrity audits, research-misconduct investigation if needed).

Adaptation Process: Monthly enrollment tracking compared to target (300-500 subjects over 6 months = 50-83 subjects/month target). If enrollment falls >20% behind target (e.g., <40 subjects/month when 50 target), Clinical-Trial Coordinator and academic partner assess reasons within 2 weeks and propose corrective action (additional sites, extended enrollment period, adjusted inclusion criteria if scientifically justified). Interim data analysis at Month 18 (2028-04-13) with 150-200 subjects provides first concordance snapshot (target ≥95% lower CI ≥93%); if concordance is 93-95% (ambiguous), additional sites or subjects are enrolled to increase power; if <93%, analytes failing concordance are escalated to Operations Committee for potential redesign or removal from final panel. Data-integrity audits (quarterly) verify protocol adherence, measurement accuracy, and absence of selective data reporting. If audit finds significant non-compliance (e.g., >5% of data entry errors, protocol deviations not documented, adverse events under-reported), study is paused; corrective actions are implemented and re-audit is conducted within 2 weeks. Any suspected research misconduct (falsified data, selective reporting) is escalated to Chief Compliance Officer within 48 hours and investigated; findings are reported to IRB and FDA within 30 days. Enrollment close-out occurs at Month 18-24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13); final analysis is completed by Month 24 (2028-10-13) and results are submitted to pre-registration database (if not already published); publication is targeted for Month 30 (2029-04-13) before FDA submission (Month 30-36 = 2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13).

Adaptation Trigger: Subject enrollment <50 subjects/month average over rolling 3-month window (proposed threshold) → protocol amendment or site-activation acceleration within 2 weeks. Interim concordance analysis (Month 18 = 2028-04-13, ≥150 subjects) shows <95% concordance (lower CI <93%) for any analyte → analyte is flagged for redesign or removal; Steering Committee is notified if >10% of Cluster 1 analytes are affected. Data-integrity audit identifies ≥5% error rate or protocol-deviation rate >3% → study is paused; corrective-action plan required and re-audit within 2-4 weeks. Suspected research misconduct or data falsification allegation → immediate escalation to Chief Compliance Officer, independent investigation, IRB and FDA notification within 30 days. Clinical-study publication delayed beyond Month 30 (2029-04-13) target by >2 months → FDA submission (target Month 30-36 = 2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13) is at risk; expedited publication or interim results submission to FDA considered.

7. Over-Claiming Prevention and Transparency/Credibility Risk Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Marketing and Claims Compliance Audit Trail (monthly review of all investor pitches, press releases, marketing materials, social media, website copy for '500 tests' claim or other unsupported assertions)
  • Monthly Analyte Performance Dashboard (published externally, updated monthly showing per-analyte pass/fail status, retired analytes with rationale)
  • External Scientific Advisory Board Meeting Minutes (quarterly public meetings, audit access to raw data, advisory recommendations on transparency)
  • Quarterly Transparency Report (to investors, regulators, clinicians: milestone status, gate results, risk updates, failed analytes, regulatory pathway, funding status)
  • Communications Policy and Compliance Checklist (prohibits '500 tests per drop' claims until ≥3 clusters independently validated; requires disclosure of retired analytes in regulatory submissions; specifies language for claims)

Frequency: Monthly marketing-materials audit (100% review of all external communications). Monthly Analyte Performance Dashboard published (internal and external to board, advisors, key stakeholders). Quarterly Transparency Report (Months 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 = 2027-04-13 onwards). Quarterly external advisory board public meetings (Months 6, 12, 18, 24 = 2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-10-13).

Responsible Role: Chief Compliance Officer (policy, audit, enforcement). CEO / Founder (communications strategy, investor messaging). Chief R&D Officer (technical accuracy of claims). External Scientific Advisory Board (independent validation of data and transparency adequacy, public credibility endorsement).

Adaptation Process: Monthly marketing-materials audit: all draft materials (investor decks, press releases, website content, social media) are reviewed by Chief Compliance Officer before publication. Any use of '500 tests', 'single drop', or other product claims is flagged; language must be verified against validated data in Analyte Performance Dashboard. If claim is not supported (e.g., Cluster 1 has only 35 analytes validated so far, not 50), material is rejected or claim is revised to 'expanding menu' or 'cumulative panel'. Pre-approved language templates are published (e.g., 'We are developing a modular panel that, when fully validated across all clusters, may eventually offer testing for up to 500 analytes'; 'Our lead panel (Cluster 1) is currently validating up to 50 analytes; we have retired X analytes due to cross-reactivity or sensitivity limitations'). Quarterly Transparency Report documents: (1) milestones achieved (analytical feasibility gate pass Month 12 = 2027-10-13, design freeze Month 18 = 2028-04-13), (2) gate results with numeric data and confidence intervals, (3) analytes retired (count and root causes: cross-reactivity, sensitivity, stability, regulatory feedback), (4) regulatory pathway and evidence status, (5) funding raised and runway to next gate. Report is published to investors quarterly and made available to scientific advisors. Any failed analyte or missed gate is reported transparently (not hidden); this builds credibility and shows rigor. External Scientific Advisory Board (5-7 members, 15+ years experience, no financial conflicts) holds quarterly public meetings (1-2 hours, virtual or in-person) where results are presented and advisory feedback is solicited. Board members have audit access to raw data (concordance, CV, shelf-life, yield data) and can verify that Analyte Performance Dashboard is accurate and complete. Board publishes quarterly statements of opinion on data integrity and transparency adequacy (e.g., 'The data presented in the dashboard is consistent with raw records reviewed; we have identified no evidence of selective reporting or data manipulation'). If Chief Compliance Officer discovers an over-claim (e.g., '500 tests per drop' used prematurely), a corrective statement is issued within 24-48 hours; the error is documented in Transparency Report; and corrective action is reported to board and investors within 1 week.

Adaptation Trigger: Any investor pitch, press release, or marketing material using '500 tests per drop' claim before ≥3 clusters are independently published and cleared (proposed threshold) → material is rejected; author is coached on policy; repeat violations result in escalation to CEO and board (proposed threshold). Monthly audit identifies unsupported claim (e.g., Cluster 1 concordance stated as '99%' when validated data shows '94%' lower CI) → corrective amendment is published within 2 weeks (proposed threshold); source of error is investigated (measurement error, data-reporting error, communication misunderstanding) and process is improved. External Scientific Advisory Board identifies data integrity concern or transparency gap (e.g., retired analytes not disclosed in Transparency Report) → Chief Compliance Officer conducts investigation within 2 weeks; findings and corrective actions are reported to board and advisors within 30 days. Media or analyst inquiry about failed analytes or over-claiming history → CEO and Chief Compliance Officer coordinate transparent response with advisory board input, emphasizing rigorous gate methodology and transparent reporting of failures; response is published and shared with investors within 1 week.

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness Confirmation: All four core governance components (internal bodies, implementation plan, decision escalation matrix, monitoring/progress) are present and detailed. However, no explicit 'Stage 1 Audit Details' file was provided in the input; the governance-phase1-audit.json describes corruption and misallocation risks but does not appear integrated into a formal audit schedule or compliance-control baseline for Months 0–6 (2026-10-13 to 2027-04-13). The audit procedures listed (quarterly gate reviews, monthly supplier scorecards, semi-annual DHF reviews, mock FDA inspection) are reactive; a foundational Month 0–1 (2026-10-13 to 2026-11-13) control-establishment schedule is absent.
  2. Internal Consistency Check: The four governance stages are logically aligned in sequence: Audit baseline → Internal Bodies established → Implementation milestones → Escalation rules → Monitoring cadence. The Steering Committee owns capital gates; Operations Committee executes; Technical Advisory Group validates; Compliance manages risk. However, one gap: the Implementation Plan step-descriptions do not explicitly state who 'formally confirms' Fallback Panel V1 analyte removals post-facto to the board monthly (vs. only reporting after Analyte Review decisions are made). This risks silent scope drift if operations removes analytes without escalating numeric impact to Steering Committee.
  3. Clarity of Roles—Advisor and Independent Perspectives: The Technical Advisory Group (external microfluidics, immunoassay, manufacturing, regulatory experts) has audit rights and can submit minority reports, but lacks formal veto authority over gate passage. The External Scientific Advisory Board (mentioned in communications policy) has audit access to raw data and quarterly public meetings, but its authority to recommend analyte removal or design changes is advisory only. Neither body has explicit authority to pause gates unilaterally. Consider: Should the Technical Advisory Group have a 'hold' veto (requiring Steering Committee override vote within 5 business days) if it identifies major feasibility risk? Should the Scientific Advisory Board have authority to request independent re-testing at any time?
  4. Process Depth—Conflict of Interest and Ethics Escalation: The Compliance, Ethics and Risk Management Committee charter defines conflict-of-interest policy and research-misconduct hotline, but does not specify: (1) How undisclosed conflicts (e.g., board member owns equity in a reagent supplier) are resolved if discovered at Month 6, 12, 18 (2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13)? (2) Who investigates and decides whether the member must recuse or divest? (3) How is the decision communicated to investors and regulators? (4) What is the timeline for resolution (within 2 weeks, 30 days)? Add explicit escalation: undisclosed material conflict → Chief Compliance Officer investigation (within 48 hours) → Steering Committee review (within 1 week) → investor board notification (within 3 business days) if impact on governance or decisions is material.
  5. Process Depth—Change Control and Design Authority Below Steering Committee: The Operations Committee approves design changes <USD 50k and <2 weeks impact without escalation. However, the implementation plan does not specify: (1) Who has signature authority on the design-change log? (2) If a microfluidics engineer proposes a cartridge geometry change (within USD 50k, <2 weeks impact), does the Chief R&D Officer sign off unilaterally, or does it require joint sign-off with Quality? (3) What happens if Operations Committee members disagree (e.g., R&D wants a design change, Quality flags risk)? Current rule is 'R&D director makes the call (subject to Steering Committee review if >USD 50k),' but that defers escalation. Add: (a) joint sign-off (R&D + Quality) required for all design changes; (b) if disagreement, escalate to Steering Committee within 3 business days; (c) no design change is implemented until sign-offs are complete.
  6. Thresholds and Delegation Clarity—'Ambiguous' Gate Results and Re-Test Authority: The monitoring plan defines 'ambiguous' results (e.g., yield 80–85% when gate is ≥85%, concordance 93–95% when gate is ≥95%) as requiring re-test and board discussion. However, the implementation plan does not specify: (1) Who decides whether a re-test is approved (Operations, Steering Committee, or board)? (2) What is the maximum duration of a re-test cycle (proposed: 2–3 weeks; if longer, escalate to Steering Committee)? (3) If re-test results remain ambiguous (e.g., yield 84–86% in second test, 95% CI 80–90%), does a third test occur or does Fallback V1 activate? Add explicit re-test rules: (a) First ambiguity → up to 2-week re-test approved by Steering Committee; (b) Second ambiguity after re-test → escalate to Steering Committee within 1 week for pass/fail/retreat vote; (c) no more than 2 re-test cycles per gate; after that, board decides by majority vote (Steering Committee or investor board if >USD 2M impact).

Tough Questions

  1. By Month 6 (2027-04-13), what is the actual measured plasma-separation efficiency from 100+ fingerstick subjects, and does the lower 95% confidence interval exceed 95% yield of ≥1.6 microliters per subject? If plasma separation is 80–90% efficiency (vs. the ≥95% gate), how many analytes are physically feasible per drop after accounting for hemolysis and clotting losses—and does this change the cumulative-menu strategy from 10 cartridges of 50 to, say, 5 cartridges of 40?
  2. Show the raw cross-reactivity screening data (each analyte pair, spiked into human plasma with elevated hemoglobin, bilirubin, lipemia, rheumatoid factor) measured at Month 6 (2027-04-13). For any analyte-pair combination showing >5% bias at 10× physiologic interferent, what is the root cause (antibody cross-binding, probe quenching, matrix interference), and is the planned remediation (antibody swap, assay chemistry redesign, or analyte removal) credible given the Months 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) timeline before design freeze?
  3. By Month 12 (2027-10-13), provide the first-article run (FAR) yield data from contract-molder partner: (1) mean yield from ≥5 batches of 1,000 cartridges each; (2) lower 95% CI for yield (gate is ≥80%); (3) any defect modes (injection-molding defects, bonding failures, reagent-fill variability) that recurred across batches; (4) if yield is <85%, what specific cartridge geometry, material, or process-window adjustment will restore it, and what is the re-tooling cost and lead-time impact?
  4. What is the current probability-weighted forecast for pharma contract revenue at Month 18 (2028-04-13)? Show the pipeline: (1) how many pharma sponsors are in active negotiation (target: 2–3 signed contracts by Month 9 = 2027-07-13); (2) what is the cumulative revenue from signed contracts by Month 12 (2027-10-13) and Month 18 (2028-04-13) (cumulative floor: USD 500k by Month 12 = 2027-10-13, USD 1M+ by Month 18 = 2028-04-13, or lean-pivot triggered); (3) if pharma revenue is tracking below USD 100k/month run-rate at Month 18 (2028-04-13), what is the plan (lean pivot, Series B timing adjustment, CLIA fallback activation)?
  5. At Month 6 (2027-04-13) FDA Pre-Submission meeting, what specific feedback will FDA provide on: (1) Is a 510(k) or De Novo pathway required for a multiplex panel of 50 analytes? (2) What analytical and clinical evidence will FDA expect (method-comparison study sample size, statistical power for 50 simultaneous analytes, outcomes data)? (3) Can staged per-cluster 510(k)s be filed, or must all analytes be submitted together? If FDA indicates De Novo is likely, how does this change the Series A/B funding roadmap (+12–18 months, +USD 2–4M)?
  6. Show the detailed unit-economics model locked by Month 6 (2027-04-13): (1) cost of goods per cartridge (bottom-up: molded body USD 2–4, fluidic bonding USD 1–2, reagents USD 4–8, QC consumables USD 2–4, packaging USD 2–3; total ≤USD 25 ceiling); (2) expected net revenue per run at each volume (1k, 10k, 50k cartridges/month) under the base-case payer scenario (USD 100–200 per panel); (3) gross margin at each volume; (4) if payers cover only USD 50–100 per panel (low scenario), what cost-reduction or volume-increase targets are needed to maintain ≥60% margin?
  7. By Month 12 (2027-10-13) analytical-feasibility gate, provide evidence that Fallback Panel V1 (50 analytes, 4–5 cartridges) is technically validated: (1) each analyte meets ≥95% concordance with reference method (show lower 95% CI for each); (2) lot-to-lot CV <10% (show data from ≥3 pilot lots); (3) shelf-life projected ≥12 months (show Arrhenius modeling with R² >0.90); (4) no analytes removed due to cross-reactivity, sensitivity, or stability failures. If >5 analytes (10% of 50) have been retired by Month 12 (2027-10-13), what is the revised Fallback Panel V1 definition, and does it still command sufficient payer interest and clinical utility to justify the USD 15–30M cumulative burn?

Summary

The governance framework establishes a disciplined four-layer structure (Steering Committee for strategy, Operations for execution, Technical Advisory Group for validation, Compliance for risk/ethics) with explicit gate-linked capital releases, quantified go/no-go criteria, and a pre-registered Fallback Product (50 analytes) retreat trigger. Monthly Analyte Review Meetings and transparency dashboards enforce credibility through public failure reporting. The framework's core strength is its defense against sunk-cost escalation: gates are quantitative (yield ≥85%, concordance ≥95%, shelf-life ≥12 months), capital tranches are tied to gate passage, and Fallback V1 retreat is pre-authorized (rather than reactive) by Month 15 (2028-01-13) if gates fail. Key gaps requiring clarification: (1) conflict-of-interest resolution timelines and escalation; (2) design-change joint sign-off authority and deadlock resolution; (3) re-test cycle limits and ambiguous-gate decision rules; (4) technical advisory board veto authority over gate passage. The regulatory pathway (510(k) vs. De Novo) is FDA Pre-Submission dependent (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) and not yet confirmed, creating material funding and timeline uncertainty. Pharma beachhead revenue is contingent and may be insufficient to avoid lean pivot by Month 18 (2028-04-13). Overall, the framework is operationally sound for a capital-constrained, high-risk medtech venture, but its success depends entirely on gate execution discipline and early resolution of regulatory pathway and pharma-revenue contingencies.

Suggestion 1 - Theranos Edison / Newark lab (cautionary precedent)

Bay Area startup claiming hundreds of tests from a fingerstick drop; operated a lab and device-development site in Newark, California. Collapsed around 2016-2018 after CMS/CLIA sanctions and fraud convictions of its founders. Documented in court records, CMS letters and journalism.

Success Metrics

Not a success: tests ran on third-party analyzers; claims not validated Outcome: CLIA sanctions, lab closure, criminal convictions, company dissolved (documented) Useful as negative benchmark for evidence transparency and peer review

Risks and Challenges Faced

Over-claiming before validation: avoid by public claim rule and pre-registered studies Sample volume physics: model drop budget (about 8-16 analytes per drop, estimate) early Closed data and no independent audit: mitigate with advisory board holding raw-data access Regulatory shortcuts via LDT route: plan CLIA and FDA evidence in parallel

Where to Find More Information

Court records and CMS CLIA inspection reports (public, search CMS and PACER) Journalism and the book 'Bad Blood' by John Carreyrou (WSJ coverage) FDA and CMS public statements on Theranos

Actionable Steps

Review CMS CLIA inspection documents for Newark lab findings to build a QMS checklist Interview former Bay Area IVD staff via LinkedIn about lessons for quality culture Consult a regulatory attorney about public-claim review process

Rationale for Suggestion

Same city, same headline claim. Directly informs credibility-first communication, evidence gates and the 'no 500 tests' claim rule. Included as a cautionary reference because validated geographic peers are few.

Suggestion 2 - Abbott i-STAT cartridge platform (Abbott Point of Care)

Handheld analyzer with single-use cartridges running blood chemistry, blood gases, cardiac markers and coagulation panels from a few drops of whole blood. Developed from the 1980s, cleared by FDA via many staged per-cartridge 510(k)s and CLIA-waived categories. Manufactured in Ottawa/Canada and US sites.

Success Metrics

Dozens of cartridge types cleared over decades (approximate, not verified) Widely deployed in hospitals, EMS and clinics worldwide Demonstrates cumulative menu via successive clearances

Risks and Challenges Faced

Cartridge reagent stability: addressed with cold-chain and room-temperature shelf-life options per cartridge Per-cartridge regulatory burden: managed through modular 510(k) sequence Sample volume limits: each cartridge serves a small analyte cluster, not hundreds

Where to Find More Information

Abbott Point of Care website (globalpointofcare.abbott) FDA 510(k) database entries for i-STAT cartridges (accessdata.fda.gov)

Actionable Steps

Pull i-STAT 510(k) summaries from FDA database to model per-cluster evidence packages Contact Abbott Point of Care business development via corporate site for partnership or licensing discussion Consult former i-STAT regulatory staff via LinkedIn as advisors

Rationale for Suggestion

Closest validated analogue to modular cartridge family with staged 510(k) clearance. Distant geographically, but shows the cumulative-menu model works at small cluster sizes.

Suggestion 3 - Cepheid GeneXpert cartridge manufacturing (Sunnyvale / Bay Area origin)

Cepheid, founded in the Bay Area, built self-contained fluidic cartridges with on-board reagent storage and a modular instrument, scaling mass cartridge production and reagent filling in-house. Acquired by Danaher in 2016. Menu grew through successive FDA clearances.

Success Metrics

Large installed base and high cartridge volumes (figures not verified) Multi-assay menu cleared incrementally Acquisition by Danaher for about USD 4B reported (approximate)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Cartridge yield at scale: solved with automated filling and in-process QC Reagent lyophilization stability: engineered dry reagent beads Capital intensity: financed via IPO and staged growth

Where to Find More Information

Actionable Steps

Approach Cepheid alumni in Sunnyvale/Bay Area via LinkedIn for manufacturing process advisors Request facility benchmarking discussions via Cepheid corporate contact Review SEC filings for capex and cartridge cost structure

Bay Area cartridge manufacturing precedent with in-house reagent filling, matching the Newark filling-site strategy and talent pool.

Secondary suggestion. Olink (Sweden, acquired by Thermo Fisher) and Quanterix (Massachusetts) built multiplex proteomics and ultrasensitive immunoassay platforms funded largely by research and pharma customers before any clinical diagnostic claims.

Success Metrics

Revenue from research and pharma customers (figures not verified) Large published datasets in peer-reviewed literature

Research-use-only versus clinical claims: kept separate Cross-reactivity in multiplex: addressed by proximity-extension design and validation publications
