  • Conduct a competitive landscape analysis and scenario plan by Month 6 (2027-04-13); identify 10–15 competitors, estimate launch dates, and model three scenarios (benign: no direct competitor by Month 36 = 2029-10-13; moderate: competitor launches 100–200 analyte panel Months 24–30 = 2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13; severe: 500-analyte competitor Months 18–24 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13); define strategic responses (accelerate clusters, pursue niches, seek partnerships) for each.
  • Quantify and document 'success' milestones with confidence intervals: at each gate (Months 6, 12, 18 = 2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13), publish pass/fail/ambiguous results with 95% CIs and decision-path (proceed, retest, redesign, retreat); define re-test protocols for ambiguous results (e.g., yield 80–85%, concordance 93–95%); board retains authority to request additional data before releasing next tranche.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • An undefined or vague Fallback Product V1 and missing retreat triggers allow sunk-cost escalation: the company continues developing unvalidated clusters past Month 18 (2028-04-13), committing USD 3–5M in Newark capital and clinical-study spend on a product that fails Month 12 (2027-10-13) gates, forcing a 6–12 month emergency redesign at 30–50% reduced valuation (USD 10–15M impact).
  • Absence of quantitative, gate-linked capital releases and board decision authority creates funding ambiguity: Series A investors do not know which tranches are at risk if gates are missed; the company either cuts spending reactively at Month 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) if gates fail (20–30% headcount cuts, US D 1–2M spend reduction) or continues unfunded development and runs out of cash, triggering 50–60% dilutive bridge financing.
  • Delayed or incomplete FDA Pre-Submission (if held after Month 6 = 2027-04-13, or missing key questions) results in misaligned regulatory strategy: the company designs clinical studies for 510(k) pathway at Months 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13), then discovers at Month 24 (2028-10-13) that FDA requires De Novo review, necessitating 12–18 additional months of clinical work, patient-reported outcomes studies, and health-economic analysis (USD 1–2M additional cost, 12–18 month delay, 20–30% Series B valuation reduction).
  • Absence of Cluster 1 definition and cross-reactivity screening allows incompatible analytes to reach pilot manufacturing: at Month 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13), high cross-reactivity in 5–10 analyte pairs is discovered, requiring removal of 20–30% of initial panel, reducing Cluster 1 from 15 to 10–12 analytes, delaying design freeze 6–8 weeks and necessitating 4-week redesign (USD 200–500k rework cost).
  • Lack of unit-economics gate and COGS ceiling locks the company into an unaffordable cartridge design: manufacturing of modular cartridges at USD 40–60 per cartridge (discovered at Month 18 = 2028-04-13) exceeds the USD 25 ceiling, making gross margin 20–40% instead of 60%, unsustainable at USD 100–200 per-run net revenue; scaling Newark facility is stranded capital (USD 2–3M loss); redesign or product pivot required (3–6 month delay, 40% Series B valuation impact).
  • No plasma-separation feasibility proof allows the company to commit to a single-drop product claim that is physically unrealizable: at Month 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13), pilot studies show plasma-separation success of 70–80% (below 95% gate), hemolysis rate >10%, or insufficient plasma volume for >5–8 simultaneous analytes; product claim becomes 'multi-drop' or 'larger sample', invalidating the single-drop differentiation and requiring 6–12 month product repositioning (USD 1–2M strategy cost, market confusion, 25–50% investor valuation downgrade).
  • Absence of clinical-study protocol design by Month 6 (2027-04-13) results in late sample-size and timeline discovery: at Month 12 (2027-10-13), enrollment planning reveals the study requires 1,500–2,000 subjects (not budgeted 300–500), extending enrollment from 6 months to 18 months (Months 12–30 = 2027-10-13 to 2029-04-13 instead of Months 12–18 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13); FDA submission moves from Month 30 (2029-04-13) to Month 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13), adding USD 1–2M to clinical-study cost and delaying clearance 6–12 months.
  • Missing payer-coverage analysis (if not completed by Month 9 = 2027-07-13) leaves revenue assumptions unvalidated: at Month 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13), payers decline coverage for a 50-analyte bundle, offering only USD 50–100 per panel (vs. modeled USD 200) because multiplex panels lack established CPT codes; per-run gross margin drops 50–80%, requiring either 3–5× sales volume (unfeasible in market) or cost reduction below USD 15 per cartridge (impossible to achieve), invalidating the business case and forcing a 40–60% Series B dilution or pivot to a narrower high-value panel (USD 5–10M fundraising impact, 12–24 month market repositioning).
  • No analyte-removal protocol or monthly performance tracking means weak analytes carry through to clinical studies: at Month 18 (2028-04-13), 5–8 analytes are discovered to have concordance 80–92% (below 95% gate), low sensitivity, or high interference, forcing post-hoc removal mid-study; FDA requires additional samples to replace them, extending enrollment 4–8 weeks; credibility is damaged by the appearance of inadequate pre-validation, and payers question the overall panel rigor.
  • Incomplete or delayed shelf-life testing (if not initiated by Month 3 = 2027-01-13) results in over-claimed shelf-life at launch: cartridges are claimed 12-month shelf-life but real-time data only covers 6–9 months; FDA pre-approval inspection (Month 36–42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13) identifies the gap, issuing a 483 observation; label must be revised to 6–8 month shelf-life post-launch, reducing competitiveness and requiring customer re-education, costing 2–3 month clearance delay and USD 500k in remediation.
  • Uncontrolled Newark capital commitment (if Tranche 1 proceeds at Month 3 = 2027-01-13 without analytical feasibility gates) risks stranded facility overhead: if yield falls to 60–70% at Month 12 (2027-10-13) and design requires significant re-work, the Newark reagent lab becomes idle, incurring USD 10–15k/month facility costs (USD 120–180k/year) with no cartridge production for 6–12 months; sunk capital of USD 500–800k is not recovered, and the company must justify continued facility lease to investors.
  • Absent supply-chain dual sourcing and risk plans result in single-point-of-failure disruptions: a critical reagent supplier discontinues an antibody at Month 18 (2028-04-13), or a contract molder loses certification; cartridge production halts for 4–8 weeks while an alternative is qualified, costing USD 100–500k in scrap, delayed clinical enrollment, and FDA-study timeline slips; with dual sourcing locked by Month 6 (2027-04-13), backup activation takes 2 weeks and costs USD 10–50k in expedite charges.

Worst Case Scenario: The startup commits substantial capital and team effort to the 500-analyte vision but discovers between Months 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) that multiple core assumptions are unachievable: plasma-separation yield is 70% instead of 95%, cross-reactivity between analyte clusters exceeds tolerances, shelf-life is only 6–8 months, cartridge yield falls to 60–70%, or payers refuse coverage for a multiplex bundle and offer only USD 50–100 per panel (vs. modeled USD 200). The company has already committed USD 3–5M to Newark facility fit-out, clinical-study enrollment, and design-freeze efforts. Without a pre-agreed Fallback V1 product or explicit retreat gates, the team and board face a late choice between (a) sinking an additional USD 2–4M into emergency redesign and hoping for a salvageable narrower product by Month 24 (2028-10-13), diluting Series B investors by 30–50%; or (b) immediately winding down and returning capital, stranding investors and destroying founder credibility. Most likely: late-stage pivot to a 50–100 analyte panel at Month 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13), requiring a 3–6 month re-validation sprint, 12–18 month delay in FDA submission, USD 20–30M cumulative burn with little or no revenue, resulting in a 50–70% valuation markdown, Series C funding collapse, and acquisition at below-cost or dissolution. The reputational damage from over-claiming (starting with 500-test marketing before evidence) is amplified by public failure, destroying clinician and payer trust for 5–10 years and blocking future fundraising in diagnostics for founder and team.

Best Case Scenario: By executing disciplined gates, transparent evidence generation, and stage-gated capital release, the startup achieves several positive outcomes by Month 48 (2030-10-13): (1) Cluster 1 (50 analytes across 4–5 cartridges) completes analytical feasibility gates by Month 12 (2027-10-13) with yield ≥85%, concordance ≥95%, and shelf-life ≥12 months; (2) Clinical studies demonstrate clinical utility and method equivalence by Month 24 (2028-10-13); (3) FDA Pre-Submission alignment by Month 6 (2027-04-13) enables a streamlined 510(k) submission at Month 30 (2029-04-13) and clearance by Month 42 (2030-04-13); (4) Newark reagent and fill facility achieves profitable operations by Month 36 (2029-10-13) at 10k cartridges/month and gross margin ≥60%; (5) Pharma contracts and grants generate USD 1–2M in pre-clearance revenue, demonstrating beachhead demand and reducing Series B dilution; (6) Published validation and advisory-board transparency establish credibility with clinicians and payers, resulting in rapid clinical-site and payer adoption post-launch; (7) First commercial sales by Month 48 (2030-10-13) with initial monthly run-rate of USD 500k–1M (5,000–10,000 cartridges); (8) Cluster 2 clinical study initiated by Month 24 (2028-10-13) and submitted by Month 36 (2029-10-13), with clearance expected by Month 42–48 (2030-04-13 to 2030-10-13), accelerating menu expansion; (9) Series B completed at competitive valuation (10–15% dilution), with clear path to profitability within 24–36 months post-clearance. Cumulative benefit: USD 50–150M in potential enterprise value by Month 60–72 (2031-10-13 to 2032-10-13), enabling acquisition by a major diagnostics player or continued growth as an independent company with positive unit economics.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If Cluster 1 analytical feasibility gates are missed at Month 12 (2027-10-13) but design reviews suggest a 3–4 month re-work cycle could resolve issues, activate a 'Design Sprint' track: pause full Newark scaling, redirect USD 500k–1M from Series A spending into a focused 12-week redesign effort (hire additional microfluidics or assay engineers, fund accelerated stability testing, conduct rapid prototyping on yield issues). Re-test at Month 15 (2028-01-13); if successful, proceed with design freeze and Newark Tranche 2 authorization at Month 18 (2028-04-13) (6-week timeline slip). If re-test fails, activate Fallback V1 by Month 16 (2028-02-13).
  • If FDA Pre-Submission outcome (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) indicates De Novo is likely (not 510(k)), immediately expand Series A Tranche 1 authorization from USD 3–4M to USD 5–6M to cover extended clinical-study, outcomes-evidence, and regulatory-consulting costs through Month 42 (2030-04-13) (12–18 month longer timeline); model Series B as a separate raise at Month 24 (2028-10-13) (vs. Month 18 = 2028-04-13) covering scale-up and market-launch readiness; adjust investor expectations upfront rather than discovering at Month 24 (2028-10-13) that De Novo requires more money and time.
  • If plasma-separation feasibility study (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) shows inadequate yield (<95%) with fingerstick-only collection, pivot to a 'microsampling device' design: partner with an established microsampling vendor (e.g., Mitra, Capitainer) to provide a home-collectable, metered-volume capillary wicking device that maintains drop-volume control and reduces hemolysis; adjust product claim from 'single fingerstick drop' to 'single collection event with self-administered microsampling device'; conduct a bridging study comparing microsampled vs. venous reference (Months 9–12 = 2027-07-13 to 2027-10-13) to demonstrate equivalence; delay design freeze 4–6 weeks but preserve the modular cartridge architecture and cost model.
  • If cross-reactivity screening (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) reveals high incompatibility in ≥5 analyte pairs, shrink Cluster 1 definition from 15 to 10–12 analytes: remove the problematic pairs and substitute lower-risk analytes with similar clinical value; maintain a 'Cluster 1 Reserve' list of candidate analytes deferred to Cluster 2; retest cross-reactivity of the reduced cluster (2–4 week effort); freeze by Month 8 (2027-06-13) and proceed to manufacturing; net effect is a slightly narrower initial menu but faster design freeze and manufacturing readiness (2–4 week timeline gain vs. trying to reformulate every incompatible pair).
  • If COGS modeling (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) shows achievable cost is USD 40–45 per cartridge (above USD 25 ceiling), pivot to a simplified 'modular cartridge with shared reader' architecture: move expensive fluidic integration into a reusable precision reader head; simplify disposable cartridge to low-cost capture strips or disks; reduce per-cartridge COGS to USD 8–12; shift manufacturing complexity to the instrument assembly partner; accept higher instrument cost (USD 50–100k vs. USD 15–30k for a simpler reader) but reduce per-run consumable cost; this trades off operator training (point-of-care deployment) and multiplexing efficiency (lower throughput per run) for unit economics. Re-design required (2–3 months) but positions the business for higher margins at lower per-run cost.
  • If payer-coverage analysis (Month 9 = 2027-07-13) shows only USD 50–100 per panel is realistic (vs. USD 200 assumed), pursue a 'high-value analyte' bundling strategy: identify the 5–10 highest-reimbursed analytes (e.g., lipid panel, metabolic panel, thyroid function); bill these individually under existing CPT codes and command premium pricing (USD 150–250 total for the core bundle); offer the remaining 40–45 analytes as 'value-add' or 'research-use' (non-billed) to drive adoption; model revenue per run at USD 100–150 (vs. USD 200 unapproved assumption) and adjust volume/profitability targets accordingly. Accept that full 50-analyte menu reimbursement may come later (18–24 months post-launch) via a bundled-CPT negotiation as real-world data accumulates. Preserve unit economics by tiering analytes, not cutting panel scope.
  • If clinical-study planning (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) reveals that sample-size calculations require 1,000+ subjects instead of 300–500, pursue a 'multi-site pooled-analysis' approach: enroll 200–300 subjects at each of 3–5 academic medical centers (Mayo, Stanford, Johns Hopkins) in parallel rather than sequential; each site starts enrollment at Month 12 (2027-10-13) and completes by Month 18–20 (2028-04-13 to 2028-06-13); pool and analyze together by Month 24 (2028-10-13); use this 'real-world multi-site perspective' to strengthen FDA package without requiring a single-site 1,000-subject study. Increases clinical complexity but compresses calendar timeline by 6–8 months.
  • If Fallback V1 is activated at Month 15 (2028-01-13) (due to missed gates), execute an accelerated '50-Analyte Core Launch' path: (1) lock Fallback V1 as the products definition—never market it as temporary; (2) conduct a streamlined clinical study (150–200 subjects, 8 weeks enrollment at Month 18–20 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-06-13) on the 50-analyte core; (3) submit a focused 510(k) by Month 27 (2029-01-13); expect clearance by Month 33–36 (2029-07-13 to 2029-10-13); (4) achieve first commercial sales by Month 42 (2030-04-13). This path sacrifices the 500-analyte headline but launches a credible, validated product 6 months earlier than the full Cluster-1-plus-expansion timeline, generating revenue sooner to fund Clusters 2+ expansion. Position Fallback V1 as 'Phase 1 of a growing menu' rather than a retreat, maintaining credibility with investors and clinicians.
  • If Newark facility costs are higher than budgeted (equipment, construction, permits), reduce Phase 1 scope: execute only the reagent-formulation and lot-release lab (USD 300–500k vs. USD 500–800k), outsource pilot cartridge-filling to a contract manufacturer at USD 5–10 per cartridge (cost for 10k cartridges = USD 50–100k). Delay full filling-line fit-out to Month 24 (2028-10-13) after revenue from cleared product supports additional capex. This spreads Newark capital over 18 months instead of 6, reducing cash-burn profile in early Series A.
  • If a well-funded competitor enters the market with a 200–300 analyte panel before Cluster 1 clears (estimated risk at Month 24–30 = 2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13), pursue a 'differentiation and partnership' strategy: (1) accelerate Cluster 2 clinical studies (initiate by Month 18 = 2028-04-13, not Month 24 = 2028-10-13) targeting a clinical niche where the competitor has not focused (e.g., rare-disease biomarkers, pediatric screening, maternal health); (2) seek a partnership or licensing deal with a large diagnostics company (Roche, Siemens, Abbott) offering exclusive access to the modular cartridge technology in exchange for upfront payment and royalties, shortening the path to broad distribution; (3) position the startup as a 'technology provider' rather than a direct competitor on the broad menu, preserving enterprise value while de-risking the head-to-head market battle.

Create Document 2: Gate Authority Charter and Capital Release Governance

ID: c59bc9a9-b64b-423c-be72-5ac82e050152

Description: Formal board resolution documenting gate criteria (Month 6, 12, 18 = 2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13), quantitative thresholds (yield >=85%, concordance >=95%, lot CV <10%, COGS <=USD 25), tranche-release decision authority (CEO draws within 2 weeks of gate closure), Fallback V1 activation protocol (automatic within 5 business days on board vote if gate fails), and escalation rules. Prevents sunk-cost escalation and drift. Primary audience: board, investors, CFO.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and Chief Executive Officer (CEO)

Primary Template: Board resolution template; corporate governance charter

Secondary Template: Venture funding document: gate-linked capital release terms

Steps to Create:

  • Define pass/fail/ambiguous gate decision rules with confidence intervals (e.g., yield 84.5% when threshold is 85% --> ambiguous, retest authorized).
  • Specify capital-release authority: CEO draws tranche within 2 weeks of gate closure; CFO countersigns for releases >USD 100k.
  • Document Fallback V1 scope (50-analyte core) and staffing contingency (-20-30% headcount, pause Newark Phase 2).
  • Set fallback activation trigger and timeline: if gate failed by Month 15 (2028-01-13), board votes within 5 business days to activate; execution within 5 days.
  • Include remediation-authorization process: if gate is 'ambiguous', approve 1-2 week retest (USD 10-20k) with defined decision rule.
  • Board vote and sign-off by Month 2 (2026-12-13); attach as board resolution.

Approval Authorities: Board of Directors (majority vote required)

Essential Information:

  • Specify the gate criteria, decision rules, and quantitative thresholds that trigger capital release or fallback activation at Months 6, 12, and 18 (2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13), including confidence intervals and re-test protocols to avoid false negatives and false positives.
  • Define the Gate Authority board resolution documenting decision ownership (CEO, CFO, board), tranche-release authority (amount, timing, countersignature requirements), and escalation rules when gates are ambiguous or fail.
  • Detail the Fallback Panel V1 scope (50-analyte core, defined by Month 1 = 2026-11-13), activation protocol (automatic board vote if gate fails by Month 15 = 2028-01-13, execution within 5 business days), and staffing/capital contingency (-20–30% headcount, pause Newark Phase 2).
  • Enumerate all quantitative gate thresholds: yield ≥85% (lower 95% CI ≥80%), lot CV <10%, concordance ≥95%, shelf-life ≥12 months projected, COGS ≤USD 25/cartridge, and specify success criteria for plasma separation (≥95% yield, hemolysis index <50) and cross-reactivity (≤5% bias at 10× interferent).
  • Document the remediation-authorization process: if a gate result is 'ambiguous' (e.g., yield 84–86% when threshold is ≥85%), define retest approval (USD 10–20k budget, 1–2 week timeline) and decision rule for retry versus fallback.
  • Specify the tranche-release schedule with gate linkage: Seed USD 2–3M (Months 0–6 = 2026-10-13 to 2027-04-13), A1 USD 3–4M (Month 6 = 2027-04-13 gate closure), A2 USD 2–3M (Month 12 = 2027-10-13 gate), A3 USD 2–3M (design freeze, by Month 18 = 2028-04-13), Series B USD 3–5M (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13), with gate-fail consequences (hold, reduce, or redirect tranche).
  • Detail capital-release mechanics: CEO draws tranche within 2 weeks of gate closure; CFO countersigns for releases >USD 100k; board approves within 5 business days of gate-closure report.
  • Define the Fallback V1 activation trigger: if gate fails and remains unresolved 4 weeks after retest or ambiguity resolution, or by Month 15 (2028-01-13) hard deadline, board votes to activate within 2 weeks; activation requires transition plan (staffing, Newark pause, Fallback V1 advancement timeline, revised funding model).
  • Specify the remediation-expense authorization: define budget for design review, re-testing, and minor redesign (USD 10–50k per cycle, max 2 cycles per gate) before fallback activation.
  • Document board governance: minimum quorum for gate votes, required sign-offs (CEO, CFO, board chair), meeting frequency (within 5 business days of gate closure), and reporting to investors (gate report includes pass/fail/ambiguous result, thresholds, data, confidence intervals, corrective action plan).
  • Include escalation rules: if gate is ambiguous and retest costs exceed USD 50k, board pre-approval required; if gate fail triggers Fallback V1 activation, CEO and board issue written communication to stakeholders (investors, FDA, team) within 5 business days.
  • Specify the gate-closure report format and distribution: quantitative data, confidence intervals, go/no-go recommendation, alternative scenarios (e.g., narrow panel, extended timeline), and financial impact; distribute to board, investors, and executive team before vote.
  • Define the fallback-transition contingency: if Fallback V1 activates, document staffing adjustment (target -20–30% headcount within 2 weeks), Newark Phase 2 pause until clinical validation complete, and revised funding plan (reduced burn, adjusted timeline to clearance for 50-analyte core).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous gate criteria (no confidence intervals) lead to subjective board decisions, enabling sunk-cost escalation and continued funding of low-likelihood technical paths; remediation: explicit thresholds with 95% CIs and re-test protocols.
  • Lack of explicit Fallback V1 scope and activation protocol results in late mission drift (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13), with 30–50% of development spend committed to analytes that fail, stranding USD 2–10 million in capital.
  • Missing tranche-release mechanics allow capital to be drawn before gate closure or withheld arbitrarily, causing cash-flow crisis or scope creep; without CEO/CFO countersignature and board vote, accountability is unclear.
  • Vague fallback-activation trigger results in repeated ambiguous gates, each triggering a 1–2 month retest cycle, extending pre-commitment period to Month 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13) without decision clarity; cost: USD 100–200k in redundant testing and delayed gate closure.
  • No remediation-budget authority creates friction between technical teams and finance; design teams over-commit on re-work budgets, CFO blocks spending, and gates slip by 2–4 weeks per cycle.
  • Lack of board-approved escalation rules means unresolved gate failures are pushed to investors or postponed, delaying Series A tranche release and causing cash-flow gap by Month 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13).
  • Missing gate-closure reporting template leads to inconsistent data presentation, making it difficult for board to compare gates, track trend (improving or worsening), and make reproducible decisions; investor confidence in governance drops 20–30%.
  • Fallback V1 not communicated to stakeholders proactively results in surprise retreat at Month 15–18 (2028-01-13 to 2028-04-13), perceived as project failure, triggering 30–50% valuation haircut and investor loss of confidence.
  • No tie between capital release and technical gates allows the company to burn through funding without evidence of progress, stretching the pre-revenue runway and increasing dilution risk at Series B (6–12 month delay, 10–20% additional dilution estimated).

Worst Case Scenario: A diagnostic device company operating without explicit gate-linked capital governance burns through USD 15–30 million across Months 0–48 (2026-10-13 to 2030-10-13) to pursue a 500-analyte moonshot that is not physically feasible. At Month 12 (2027-10-13), analytical feasibility tests show yield is 78% (below ≥85% gate) and cross-reactivity affects 35% of analyte pairs (far above acceptable); however, no pre-agreed Fallback Product exists. The team argues for 'a few more months of optimization,' the board lacks a decision framework and capital has not been explicitly linked to gates, so spending continues. By Month 18 (2028-04-13), another USD 2–3 million has been spent on redesign; shelf-life data reveal only 8 months' stability, incompatible with commercial claims. The company has burned USD 10–12 million and is still pre-product. Investors, having seen no gate-closure reports or objective milestones, lose confidence and delay Series B. Newark capital of USD 500–800 k has been spent on reagent space, now underutilized. By Month 24 (2028-10-13), funding dries up or requires a down round at 50% valuation, diluting founders and early investors by 20–30%. The company pivots to a 50-analyte panel 18 months late, missing the regulatory window, and is acquired or shut down within 3–6 months. Total loss: USD 15–30 million, 3–4 year delay to market, and credibility damage reinforcing skepticism about single-drop diagnostics.

Best Case Scenario: A governance-disciplined diagnostics startup defines explicit gate criteria and capital tranches at Month 1 (2026-11-13), with a pre-registered Fallback Panel V1 (50 analytes) as the guaranteed product. Each gate (Months 6, 12, 18 = 2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13) closes with a board vote within 5 business days, comparing actual data against pre-set thresholds with confidence intervals. When Month 12 (2027-10-13) analyte testing shows yield of 86% (±2%, 95% CI 84–88%, passes ≥85%), concordance 96%, shelf-life 13 months, and COGS USD 24.50, the board releases Series A Tranche 2 (USD 2–3 million) within 2 weeks. Newark Phase 2 fill-line capital (USD 2–3 million) is authorized at Month 18 (2028-04-13) after design freeze and ISO 13485 certification. Clinical studies enroll 300 subjects by Month 18 (2028-04-13), and FDA Pre-Submission feedback (obtained Month 6 = 2027-04-13) confirms the 510(k) pathway is viable. By Month 30 (2029-04-13), the 510(k) submission is filed with clean analytical and clinical data; by Month 36 (2029-10-13), clearance is issued. First commercial sales launch Month 48 (2030-10-13). The company has raised Seed + Series A (USD 10–12 million) plus USD 1–2 million in grants, managed burn efficiently, and avoided both false-negative retreat and sunk-cost escalation. The Fallback V1 plan is never needed because gates are met and progression is evidence-based. Cluster 2 is greenlit by Month 36 (2029-10-13) and cleared by Month 42 (2030-04-13). By Month 60 (2031-10-13), three clusters (150 analytes) are on the market, revenue is USD 8–12 million annually, and a Series B (USD 3–5 million) is raised at premium valuation based on demonstrated execution and regulatory success. Credibility is high because results match pre-registered gates and the company publishes data transparently.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If explicit gate thresholds cannot be pre-agreed by Month 2 (2026-12-13), engage an independent clinical advisor (academic clinical-research partner or regulatory consultant) to define thresholds in a neutral workshop (2–3 days) and document them as a board-endorsed 'Gate Charter,' approved at an emergency board meeting. Cost: USD 10–20 k; delay: 2–4 weeks. This bypasses internal debate and locks in objective criteria.
  • If the board is reluctant to authorize automatic Fallback V1 activation, establish a 'Fallback Review Committee' (subset of board + CEO + CFO) that meets within 5 business days of gate failure and makes the activate/remediate decision in writing within 2 weeks; document the decision rationale and communicate to investors. This distributes accountability and accelerates gate resolution without full board delay.
  • If tranche-release authority is unclear, appoint a 'Capital Committee' (board chair, CEO, CFO, one investor representative) with delegated authority to approve tranches up to USD 3 million within 5 business days of gate closure, with board ratification at the next regular meeting. This speeds capital release and reduces cash-flow gap risk.
  • If gate-closure reports are inconsistent across gates, template a standard 'Gate Closure Report' (2–3 pages: gate criteria, data, 95% CIs, pass/fail/ambiguous result, alternative actions, financial impact, board recommendation) and require the VP of Operations or Quality/Regulatory lead to complete it within 2 business days of gate closure. Standardization improves board clarity and investor confidence.
  • If a gate result is persistently ambiguous (e.g., yield 84–86% over three re-tests with 95% CIs overlapping the threshold), establish a tiebreaker rule: the board votes on 'Proceed with Remediation' (allocate USD 20–30 k for a focused 2-week design sprint) or 'Activate Fallback V1' (within 5 days). The tiebreaker forces a decision and prevents indefinite re-testing loops.
  • If remediation costs exceed USD 50 k per gate cycle, require pre-approval from the board or Capital Committee before spend, submitted at the same time as the gate-closure report. This prevents scope creep in re-work and keeps the board informed of emerging costs.
  • If the Fallback V1 scope is unclear, conduct a 'Minimum Viable Product (MVP) workshop' in Month 1 (2026-11-13) with R&D, product, and commercial leads to define the 50-analyte core and publish it in the 'Fallback V1 Specification' document, approved by the board. This front-loads the choice and avoids late debate.
  • If Newark capital-release authority is contested (design-team wants early fit-out; CFO wants to wait for gates), establish a 'Newark Investment Governance' protocol specifying that Phase 1 (USD 500–800 k, reagent lab) is released at Month 6 (2027-04-13) gate closure if plasma-separation and cross-reactivity gates pass; Phase 2 (USD 2–3 M, filling line) is released at Month 18 (2028-04-13) design-freeze gate. Lock this in the board charter by Month 1 (2026-11-13).
  • If investors demand visibility into gate decisions before formal board meetings, publish a 'Gate Scorecard' (one-page dashboard: gate name, criteria, actual results, 95% CI, pass/fail, timestamp) to the investor portal within 24 hours of gate closure, with full Gate Closure Report to follow within 5 business days. This satisfies investor need for timely updates without delaying formal approval.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Lack of scenario sensitivity analysis means the board and investors cannot understand downside risk; if burn rate increases by 20% or pharma revenue is 50% below forecast, the impact on runway and breakeven is unknown, increasing surprise risk at Months 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13).
  • Headcount-ramp assumptions (25–35 by Month 12 = 2027-10-13, estimate) not linked to project milestones can result in hiring faster or slower than needed; over-hiring burns cash; under-hiring delays technical work and misses gates, pushing timelines 2–4 months and requiring Series B acceleration.
  • Absence of a clear lean-pivot trigger and contingency spending plan leaves management and board without a pre-agreed path if pharma contracts fail or core technical gates are missed; ambiguity delays decision-making and allows sunk-cost escalation, burning USD 1–3 million in unproductive spend before retreat is acknowledged.

Worst Case Scenario: The company enters Phase 2 (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) on track with analytical feasibility gates passed, but discovers that clinical-study enrollment is 40–50% slower than projected due to site activation delays or patient-recruitment challenges. Simultaneously, a key equipment supplier announces a 6-month extension of lead times, pushing Newark filling-line delivery from Month 18 (2028-04-13) to Month 24 (2028-10-13). Pharma contracts, expected to deliver USD 500 k by Month 18 (2028-04-13), materialize at only USD 150 k due to partner delays. The cash burn continues at USD 800–1000 k/month (estimate). Runway from Month 18 (2028-04-13) Series A Tranche 3 (USD 2–3 million) is exhausted by Month 21–22 (2029-01-13 to 2029-02-13). The company faces a USD 2–4 million funding gap and must either cut 30–40% of headcount (demolishing technical progress), pause Newark build-out and abandon the manufacturing timelines, or seek emergency bridge financing at a 40–50% valuation discount (estimate), diluting existing investors by 10–20% (estimate). The combination strands USD 500–800 k in partial Newark equipment and clinical-study setup costs, delays design freeze to Month 24 (2028-10-13) or later, pushes FDA submission from Month 30 (2029-04-13) to Month 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13), and reduces investor confidence in execution, increasing Series B difficulty and lowering valuation by 30–50% (estimate). Total impact: 12–18 month program delay, USD 3–8 million in stranded capital and unplanned dilution, and significant reputational damage with investors and partners.

Best Case Scenario: The cash-flow model is detailed and accurate, with conservative burn-rate assumptions (USD 10 million Months 0–18 = 2026-10-13 to 2028-04-13 vs. USD 12 million high case, estimate), enabling Seed and Series A tranches to be sized confidently and released on schedule at gates. Pharma partnerships materialize as planned: first USD 50–100 k contract signed by Month 9 (2027-07-13), cumulative USD 1–2 million by Month 24 (2028-10-13). Analytical feasibility gates are met on schedule at Months 6 and 12 (2027-04-13 and 2027-10-13), unlocking Tranche 1 and 2 capital releases and sustaining headcount ramp to 35 staff by Month 12 (2027-10-13) and 60 staff by Month 24 (2028-10-13). FDA Pre-Submission at Month 6 (2027-04-13) aligns on a 510(k) pathway (not De Novo), confirming Series B sizing at USD 3–5 million is adequate. Clinical study enrollment achieves target by Month 18 (2028-04-13), data analysis completes by Month 24 (2028-10-13), publication is achieved by Month 30 (2029-04-13), and FDA submission occurs on schedule at Month 30 (2029-04-13). Clearance is received by Month 42 (2030-04-13), enabling first commercial sales by Month 48 (2030-10-13). Total cumulative funding raised is USD 8–12 million (Seed and Series A), supplemented by USD 1–2 million in pharma/grants, meeting the estimated USD 15–30 million burn through clearance within the committed range. Board confidence remains high throughout; Series B fundraising for Phase 3 (clinical expansion and manufacturing scale-up) is completed by Month 24 (2028-10-13) at a strong valuation, and the company is on track for profitability by Month 60 (2031-10-13) or earlier.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If detailed monthly burn-rate modeling proves too resource-intensive or data-sparse in the first few weeks, conduct a simplified quarterly cash model (Months 0–3 = 2026-10-13 to 2027-01-13, 3–6, 6–12 = 2026-10-13 to 2027-01-13, 2027-01-13 to 2027-04-13, 2027-04-13 to 2027-10-13) with payroll, major capex, and gate-triggered contingencies. Upgrade to monthly detail by Month 3 (2027-01-13) once actual spend data are available.

Present both to Series A leads and let them choose their preferred risk profile.

This reduces the risk of later Series B upsizing.

Create Document 4: FDA Regulatory Pathway and Clinical Study Strategy

ID: 59c426ca-1014-4922-9849-a29d5a0e8b4d

Description: Documentation of FDA Pre-Submission feedback (held by Month 6 = 2027-04-13), confirmed regulatory pathway (510(k) vs. De Novo), clinical-study protocol (sample size, reference methods, primary endpoints, comparators), and pre-registration on ClinicalTrials.gov. Includes De Novo contingency modeling if applicable. Primary audience: regulatory lead, R&D, clinical team, board. Drives clinical evidence generation and submission timeline.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Quality Officer / Regulatory Affairs Lead (with FDA regulatory consultant support)

Primary Template: FDA guidance on 510(k) and De Novo submissions; IVD clinical validation guidance

Secondary Template: Clinical study protocol template (ICH-GCP compliant); ClinicalTrials.gov registration protocol

Steps to Create:

  • Prepare FDA Pre-Submission Type B meeting package (Months 2-3 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-01-13) with regulatory questions: 510(k) vs. De Novo likelihood; clinical evidence expectations; tiered submission strategy feasibility.
  • Hold Pre-Submission by Month 6 (2027-04-13); document FDA feedback in writing.
  • Draft two clinical-study protocols in parallel: Protocol A (510(k) focus, analytical concordance, 200-300 subjects) and Protocol B (De Novo focus, clinical utility, 400-500 subjects).
  • Lock primary endpoints (e.g., concordance >=95% with reference, CV <10%, accuracy >=95%).
  • Specify sample size and statistical power; register protocol on ClinicalTrials.gov before enrollment begins.
  • Model both 510(k) and De Novo timelines; if De Novo is likely, confirm Series B expansion plan.
  • Finalize protocol by Month 9 (2027-07-13); begin enrollment Month 12 (2027-10-13).

Approval Authorities: Chief Quality Officer, FDA (via Pre-Submission response), Institutional Review Board (IRB), Clinical Research Partner

Essential Information:

  • Obtain FDA Pre-Submission Type B meeting feedback by Month 6 (2027-04-13) that clarifies: (1) whether 510(k) or De Novo is the likely regulatory pathway for a multiplex panel claiming 50–100 simultaneous analytes; (2) what analytical evidence (method-comparison studies, accuracy, precision, concordance) FDA expects; (3) whether tiered/successive cluster submissions are acceptable or if all 500 analytes must be cleared together; (4) what clinical utility evidence is required (patient-relevant outcomes vs. analytical performance alone); (5) whether a CLIA lab-service route can launch in parallel without prejudicing device submissions.
  • Draft and lock two parallel clinical-study protocols by Month 9 (2027-07-13)—one optimized for 510(k) (Protocol A: analytical concordance focus, 200–300 subjects) and one for De Novo (Protocol B: clinical utility focus, 400–500 subjects, patient-relevant outcomes)—specifying sample size, statistical power (80% for primary endpoints at alpha=0.05), reference methods, primary endpoints (concordance ≥95%, CV <10%, accuracy ≥95% per analyte), and success/failure criteria before enrollment begins.
  • Pre-register the selected clinical-study protocol on ClinicalTrials.gov (required by FDA for credibility and transparency) and obtain Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval before Month 12 (2027-10-13) enrollment initiation.
  • Establish which submission strategy is most feasible and lowest-cost: (a) staged per-analyte or per-cluster 510(k)s (separate submissions, faster, easier regulatory pathway) vs. (b) single comprehensive De Novo (all analytes in one submission, higher evidence bar, 12–18 months longer), based on FDA Pre-Submission response; model both timelines and funding needs in the Series A and Series B plans.
  • If FDA indicates De Novo is likely, expand Series B funding projection by an additional USD 2–4M and extend clinical-study runway by 6–12 months (clearance moves from Months 36–48 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-10-13 to Months 48–66 = 2030-10-13 to 2032-04-13); communicate this to investors by Month 9 (2027-07-13) so funding strategy can be adjusted.
  • Specify the clinical study design: site selection (3–5 clinical sites in different geographic regions for enrollment resilience), subject population (healthy and disease states), sample size justification (power calculation accounting for Bonferroni correction if >15 analytes), paired sample collection (fingerstick device sample + reference laboratory sample from same subject), reference methods for each analyte (established clinical laboratory methods or FDA-cleared comparators), and data-analysis plan (per-analyte concordance, Bland–Altman plots, accuracy within pre-specified tolerances).
  • Define the go/no-go decision rules for the clinical study: if any analyte shows concordance <93% (lower 95% confidence interval) at interim analysis (Month 18 = 2028-04-13), decide to (1) redesign assay and re-test (4–8 weeks), (2) remove from initial submission and list as 'evaluated and not included', or (3) defer to Cluster 2; document all decisions in the submission package for FDA.
  • Develop a contingency regulatory strategy if FDA issues Major Deficiencies on the initial 510(k)/De Novo submission (expected timing Month 36–42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13): specify timeline for response (typically 2–6 months), what additional data or studies may be requested, and identify pivots (e.g., narrowing the analyte menu, adding clinical-utility data, conducting additional method-comparison studies).
  • Create a project timeline integrating regulatory and clinical milestones: FDA Pre-Submission Months 2–6 (2026-12-13 to 2027-04-13), protocol lock Month 9 (2027-07-13), IRB approval Months 10–12 (2027-08-13 to 2027-10-13), clinical enrollment Months 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13), data analysis and report Month 24 (2028-10-13), manuscript submission Month 24–30 (2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13), FDA submission Month 30 (2029-04-13), with decision milestones at Months 36, 42, 48 (2029-10-13, 2030-04-13, 2030-10-13).
  • Quantify the budget for regulatory and clinical work: FDA Pre-Submission meeting preparation and consulting USD 50–100k (Months 2–6 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-04-13); clinical protocol development USD 30–50k; clinical study execution (site initiation, enrollment, reference-lab testing, data management, analysis, publication support) USD 2–4M over Months 12–36 (2027-10-13 to 2029-10-13); regulatory consulting and submission preparation USD 200–500k over Months 24–36 (2028-10-13 to 2029-10-13); total regulatory and clinical budget USD 2.3–4.7M.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Without FDA Pre-Submission alignment by Month 6 (2027-04-13), the company may invest 12–18 months in study design, recruitment, and testing only to discover that FDA expects different evidence (e.g., clinical utility rather than analytical concordance), forcing major redesign or re-study that adds 6–12 months and USD 1–2M in unplanned work.
  • If the clinical-study protocol is not pre-registered and locked by Month 9 (2027-07-13), FDA may view the study as exploratory post-hoc analysis rather than prospective validation, reducing credibility and potentially delaying clearance by 3–6 months or triggering a Refuse to File (RTF) action.
  • Uncertainty between 510(k) and De Novo pathways until Month 12 (2027-10-13) or later prevents accurate Series A/B funding sizing. A late discovery that De Novo is required adds USD 2–4M in budget and 12–18 months to timeline, forcing emergency funding or scope retreat at inopportune times.
  • Inadequate sample size or statistical power in the clinical study (e.g., <150 subjects for 50-analyte panel) results in insufficient evidence to support FDA approval, requiring repeat studies that cost USD 500k–1M and delay clearance 12–18 months.
  • If clinical-study sites are concentrated in one geographic region and a public-health or regulatory event disrupts enrollment (e.g., pandemic, regional FDA inspection), enrollment may slip by 3–6 months, cascading delays to analysis, publication, and submission.
  • Missing or incomplete clinical data (e.g., reference-method results incomplete for 5–10% of subjects, or paired samples uncollected) delays data-lock and analysis by 4–8 weeks per issue and may invalidate analytes with sparse data, reducing the claimed analyte count.
  • Failure to document the regulatory decision-making process (which analytes pass, which fail, why) in the submission package leaves FDA without visibility into the company's rigor and invites requests for additional studies or data.
  • Without a De Novo contingency plan communicated to investors by Month 9 (2027-07-13), discovering at Month 18 (2028-04-13) that FDA signals De Novo surprises Series A investors who budgeted for 510(k)-only runway, triggering funding shortfall and forced scope cuts or down-round.
  • If clinical results show weaker-than-expected concordance (90–93% instead of ≥95%) for some analytes and the company has no pre-agreed removal/redesign protocol, ambiguity about how to proceed delays FDA submission 2–4 months while internal debate resolves.
  • Submission to FDA without publication of clinical results (or with publication delayed beyond submission) reduces external validation and may invite FDA to request independent replication or pre-approval inspections that add 2–4 months.

Worst Case Scenario: Discovery at Month 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13) that FDA will require De Novo pathway and comprehensive clinical-utility studies (not just analytical concordance) forces redesign of the entire clinical-study plan, expands required sample size to 500–1,000 subjects, extends enrollment by 12–18 months, requires additional funding of USD 3–5M beyond Series A, delays first FDA submission from Month 30 (2029-04-13) to Month 42–48 (2030-04-13 to 2030-10-13), and pushes product clearance beyond Month 60 (2031-10-13). Simultaneously, competitors may launch similar multiplex devices, eroding market opportunity and valuation. Combined impact: USD 3–5M funding gap at Month 24 (2028-10-13) requiring down-round financing or scope retreat; 12–18 month timeline slip; credibility damage from initial regulatory miscalculation; and reduced product differentiation by launch. Worst case valuation impact: 30–50% writedown.

Best Case Scenario: FDA Pre-Submission feedback at Month 6 (2027-04-13) confirms that staged per-cluster 510(k) pathway is acceptable, analytical-concordance evidence is sufficient (clinical-utility studies not required upfront), and a tiered strategy beginning with 50-analyte Cluster 1 is aligned with FDA's expectations. Clinical protocol is locked by Month 9 (2027-07-13), IRB approval obtained by Month 12 (2027-10-13), enrollment reaches 300 subjects by Month 18 (2028-04-13), interim analysis shows concordance ≥95% for all analytes, and final data lock occurs by Month 24 (2028-10-13). Publication in a peer-reviewed journal by Month 30 (2029-04-13) demonstrates independent validation. First 510(k) submission is filed Month 30 (2029-04-13) with complete, high-quality clinical data, FDA grants clearance by Month 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13) without deficiencies, and first commercial sales begin by Month 48 (2030-10-13) with strong clinician and payer confidence. Series B funding is secured on favorable terms because regulatory pathway is de-risked and clinical evidence is published. Cluster 2 regulatory strategy is also clarified, enabling planning for expansion. Best case impact: on-time regulatory and commercial execution; investor confidence strengthened 20–30% (valuation uplift); competitive advantage sustained; pathway to 500-analyte menu credible by Months 90+ (2034-04-13+).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If FDA Pre-Submission cannot be held by Month 6 (2027-04-13) due to FDA scheduling delays, request an expedited meeting or written feedback by Month 9 (2027-07-13), and begin protocol development in parallel assuming the more conservative De Novo pathway (larger sample, clinical-utility focus). This adds cost and timeline uncertainty but avoids blocking development.
  • If De Novo appears likely by Month 9 (2027-07-13), immediately pivot to an expanded clinical-study design (Protocol B, 500 subjects, patient-relevant outcomes) and adjust Series B funding plan upward by USD 2–3M; communicate revised timeline to investors by Month 12 (2027-10-13) before Series A tranche 2 is released, allowing them to plan Series B with full context.
  • If clinical-study enrollment is slower than projected (e.g., <100 subjects enrolled by Month 18 = 2028-04-13 instead of projected 150–200), conduct an interim analysis at Month 18 (2028-04-13) using available data, publish preliminary results to build credibility, and extend enrollment by 6 months (to Month 24 = 2028-10-13) while proceeding with FDA submission using interim data, requesting FDA feedback on acceptability of interim results.
  • If early clinical data suggest that 5–10 analytes from Cluster 1 have concordance <93%, remove those analytes immediately (no re-design attempt), document removal with root-cause analysis, and proceed with a 40–45 analyte Cluster 1 instead, positioning removals as evidence of rigorous validation rather than product failure. This shortens timeline and preserves credibility.
  • If clinical sites cannot be activated by Month 12 (2027-10-13) due to contracting delays, substitute a contract research organization (CRO) partner to manage enrollment, increasing study cost by USD 200–300k but compressing activation timeline from 3–4 months to 4–6 weeks. This is costlier but de-risks timeline.
  • If publication of clinical results is delayed beyond Month 30 (2029-04-13) due to peer-review cycles, submit the FDA 510(k) package with the manuscript under review (status: 'in preparation' or 'under peer review') and commit to providing the published version within 60 days of clearance. FDA typically accepts in-review manuscripts if the data package is solid.
  • If FDA issues Major Deficiencies on the initial submission (expected timeline Month 36–42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13), prioritize deficiency response within 2–3 months, identify which deficiencies can be addressed with existing data and which require new studies, and distinguish between (a) deficiencies that are substantive (e.g., concordance for one analyte is 92%, not ≥95%) vs. (b) administrative/documentation deficiencies that are resolved by re-analysis or clarification. Allocate budget and timeline accordingly: substantive deficiencies cost USD 500k–1M and add 2–4 months; administrative deficiencies cost USD 50–100k and add 2–4 weeks.
  • If competitors launch before this company's clearance, pivot narrative to emphasize independent validation, transparent data publication, and scientific credibility rather than speed-to-market. Publish clinical results even before clearance (peer-reviewed journals) to differentiate on evidence quality, potentially accelerating payer coverage and adoption post-launch despite competitive entry.

Create Document 5: Cluster 1 Analyte Specification and Cross-Reactivity Validation Plan

ID: d4ce15cf-caf1-47ff-b185-183f2abc2e17

Description: Formal definition of Cluster 1 (10-15 analytes with clinical rationale for each, selected for low known cross-reactivity risk, established reference methods). Includes comprehensive cross-reactivity matrix protocol (spiked plasma with hemoglobin, bilirubin, lipemia, rheumatoid factor at 10x physiologic; acceptance <=5% bias). Specifies execution timeline (Months 3-6 = 2027-01-13 to 2027-04-13), acceptance criteria, and Analyte Removal Log process. Primary audience: assay chemistry lead, R&D, quality, FDA.

Responsible Role Type: Director of Assay Chemistry and Analytical Science

Primary Template: Analytical method validation protocol template; assay development SOP

Secondary Template: FDA guidance on multiplex device validation; ISO/IEC 17043 proficiency testing

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 1 (2026-11-13), propose Cluster 1 candidates (10-15 analytes) with literature cross-reactivity risk assessment per pair.
  • By Month 2 (2026-12-13), finalize Cluster 1 list and specify multiplex reagent formulation (pH, osmolality, stabilizers, storage).
  • Design comprehensive cross-reactivity matrix: measure each analyte alone and in full plex, spiked with hemoglobin (200 mg/dL), bilirubin (5 mg/dL), triglycerides (500 mg/dL), rheumatoid factor (100 IU/mL) at up to 10x physiologic. Acceptance: <=5% bias from any interferent, >=95% concordance singleplex.
  • Execute study Months 3-6 (2027-01-13 to 2027-04-13); document all results, failures, and root causes.
  • Prepare Analyte Removal Log: for any analyte pair failing <=5% bias, document failure reason, reformulation attempt (if any), and removal justification for FDA submission.
  • Lock final Cluster 1 by Month 6 (2027-04-13) gate; update clinical-study protocol if analytes are removed.

Approval Authorities: Director of Assay Chemistry, Chief Quality Officer, Chief Technical Officer, FDA (via Pre-Submission feedback)

Essential Information:

  • Specify the exact 10–15 analytes that comprise Cluster 1, with clinical rationale for each choice, published reference ranges, and established reference methods (e.g., LC-MS/MS, immunoassay).
  • Define the multiplex reagent formulation (pH, osmolality, stabilizers, protease inhibitors, antimicrobial preservatives, storage temperature and duration) and justify selection based on cross-reactivity risk.
  • Conduct a systematic cross-reactivity matrix study: measure each analyte singly, in pairs, and in full plex (10–15 analytes) using spiked human plasma with physiologic and supra-physiologic levels of known interferents (hemoglobin, bilirubin, triglycerides, rheumatoid factor, heterophile antibodies, hemolysis mimics) at 1×, 5×, and 10× physiologic concentrations.
  • Establish acceptance criteria and success metrics: ≤5% bias from any single interferent at 10× physiologic; ≥95% concordance singleplex vs. multiplex; <10% CV within run and between runs; detection limits and linear range per analyte meeting clinical requirements.
  • Document all cross-reactivity failures, root causes, and remediation: for any analyte pair or triplet failing the ≤5% bias threshold, specify whether the pair is removed from Cluster 1, reformulated (antibody swap, pH adjustment, reagent concentration change), or deferred to Cluster 2.
  • Create an Analyte Removal Log that tracks each candidate analyte's fate (pass/fail/ambiguous/reformulation pending) and justification for FDA Pre-Submission submission and eventual 510(k) documentation.
  • Specify the execution timeline: analyte candidate list by Month 2 (2026-12-13); formulation design by Month 2 (2026-12-13); cross-reactivity study initiation Month 3 (2027-01-13); interim data review Months 4–5 (2027-02-13 to 2027-03-13); final Cluster 1 lock by Month 6 (2027-04-13) gate; analyte-removal decisions documented by Month 6 (2027-04-13).
  • Quantify the analyte-loss assumption: assume 10–20% of initial candidates fail thresholds; Cluster 1 target is 10–15 passing analytes; if >30% fail, post-mortem on initial selection or threshold realism before proceeding to clinical studies.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or incorrect analyte-pair cross-reactivity testing: undetected interferent pairs during development are discovered in clinical studies or post-launch, forcing assay redesigns, 3–6 month delays, and USD 200–500k rework.
  • Missing interferent classes (e.g., neglect of heterophile antibodies or lipemia at supra-physiologic levels): analyte accuracy drifts in real-world samples, affecting payer coverage and clinical adoption.
  • Lack of analyte-removal documentation: removed analytes are omitted from FDA submission without justification, triggering FDA requests for additional data and delaying clearance by 2–4 months.
  • Unclear reformulation protocols: when an analyte pair fails, the document does not specify whether it is reformulated, by whom, and on what timeline; reformulation is delayed or abandoned without decision.
  • Vague success criteria: 'low cross-reactivity' is undefined; without explicit ≤5% bias and ≥95% concordance thresholds, ambiguous results are misinterpreted or ignored, propagating weak analytes to clinical studies.
  • Failure to lock Cluster 1 by Month 6 (2027-04-13) gate: delays analytical feasibility gate, pushes design freeze to Month 24–30 (2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13), and shifts Newark commitment and clinical studies downstream, extending total program by 6–12 months.
  • No interim data review or decision points between Months 3–6 (2027-01-13 to 2027-04-13): data accumulates without action, and by Month 6 (2027-04-13) the company discovers 50%+ analyte-pair failures with no time for reformulation, forcing scope retreat without evidence.
  • Failure to record assumptions or formulation rationale: future modifications are made blindly, re-introducing cross-reactivity that was previously optimized out.

Worst Case Scenario: At Month 6 (2027-04-13), the cross-reactivity study reveals that 40–60% of analyte pairs fail the ≤5% bias acceptance criterion due to antibody cross-binding, matrix effects, or reagent instability. Because the study design was incomplete or criteria were ambiguous, the company cannot distinguish between fixable (reformulation, antibody swap) and unfixable (remove analyte) failures. The team proposes 4–6 week reformulation cycles for multiple analytes, but this delays Cluster 1 lock to Month 9–12 (2027-07-13 to 2027-10-13). Meanwhile, clinical-study initiation slips from Month 12 (2027-10-13) to Month 15–18 (2028-01-13 to 2028-04-13), and FDA Pre-Submission feedback (conditional on Cluster 1 analyte list) is unavailable. Newark Phase 1 capital is released at Month 6 (2027-04-13) on the assumption Cluster 1 is locked, but the reagent lab's utility is unclear if analyte composition is unsettled. By Month 12 (2027-10-13), the analytical feasibility gate cannot be held because cross-reactivity work is incomplete. Series A funding is delayed or conditioned on resolving cross-reactivity, creating a USD 2–4 million funding gap at Month 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13). Cumulative impact: 4–9 month timeline slip, USD 2–4 million emergency fundraising or spending cuts, 30–50% valuation haircut due to missed milestones, and loss of investor confidence in technical execution. Credibility is further eroded by public perception of weak data management if cross-reactivity failures are disclosed without clear remediation.

Best Case Scenario: A well-designed, pre-registered Cluster 1 Specification and Cross-Reactivity Validation Plan enables rapid, disciplined assay development. By Month 2 (2026-12-13), the team defines 15 candidate analytes with clinical rationale and publishes the plan with pre-agreed acceptance criteria (≤5% bias, ≥95% concordance). Months 3–5 (2027-01-13 to 2027-03-13) cross-reactivity testing identifies 2–3 analyte pairs that fail, each with clear root cause. By Month 5 (2027-03-13), reformulation or removal decisions are made within 2–3 weeks per analyte. Cluster 1 is locked at 12–13 passing analytes by Month 6 (2027-04-13). The Analyte Removal Log documents the two failed pairs and reformulation rationale, and this log is part of FDA Pre-Submission package. Clinical-study protocol is finalized by Month 8–9 (2027-06-13 to 2027-07-13), enrollment begins Month 12 (2027-10-13) on schedule. The analytical feasibility gate at Month 12 (2027-10-13) passes with high confidence because cross-reactivity work is complete. Series A capital is released on time; Newark Phase 1 fit-out proceeds without design uncertainty. FDA feedback from Pre-Submission is incorporated into the clinical study and submission package. By Month 18 (2028-04-13), design freeze is achievable because Cluster 1 is fully characterized. Cumulative impact: on-time delivery of Cluster 1 by Month 6 (2027-04-13), clear evidence trail for FDA, elimination of 3–6 month delays, USD 500k–1 million in avoidable rework prevented, and sustained investor confidence. The successful cross-reactivity plan becomes a template for Clusters 2–5, compressing future cluster development by 20–30%.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Simplify and risk-reduce: narrow Cluster 1 to 8 analytes (instead of 10–15) chosen for extreme cross-reactivity compatibility and well-established reference methods; conduct the same cross-reactivity matrix but with smaller scope (2–3 week reduction in timeline). Accept smaller initial menu in exchange for higher analytical confidence. Lock Cluster 1 by Month 6 (2027-04-13) gate; start with proven assays, add difficulty later.
  • Use external analyte-selection and validation partner: engage a CRO or academic lab (e.g., Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic) to design and execute the cross-reactivity study (Months 3–6 = 2027-01-13 to 2027-04-13) while the internal R&D team focuses on cartridge and reagent formulation. Accelerates testing and leverages external expertise; cost USD 200–400k. Ensures independent, published-grade data early.
  • Staged analyte lock: by Month 2 (2026-12-13), identify 5 'anchor' analytes (highest clinical value, lowest cross-reactivity risk) and lock these immediately. By Month 4 (2027-02-13), test the anchor 5 in plex; by Month 6 (2027-04-13), confirm stability and concordance. Independently, test 5–10 'expansion' analytes in parallel; add them to Cluster 1 only if cross-reactivity passes by Month 6 (2027-04-13). Allows partial Cluster 1 lock by Month 6 (2027-04-13) even if expansion analytes are ambiguous.
  • Pre-qualify critical analyte pairs using literature and supplier data: by Month 1 (2026-11-13), assemble published cross-reactivity matrices for antibodies from vendors and academic literature. Identify 3–5 analyte pairs with known or likely incompatibility. Remove those pairs from Cluster 1 before experimental testing, reducing the test matrix by 20–30% and shortening Months 3–6 (2027-01-13 to 2027-04-13) work by 1–2 weeks.
  • Defer cross-reactivity to clinical study: if Cluster 1 analytes cannot be fully tested against all interferents by Month 6 (2027-04-13), proceed with the top 10 passing analytes in clinical study. Run clinical samples paired with reference methods and measure bias in real-world matrices (captures in-vivo interferents like hemolysis, lipemia, icterus naturally). Accept slower clinical enrollment (add 4–6 weeks to detect interferent failures) in exchange for compressed pre-clinical timeline. Use clinical data for FDA submission evidence of cross-reactivity control.
  • Prioritize and gate analyte testing: by Month 3 (2027-01-13), run cross-reactivity testing on the 5 analytes with highest clinical value and lowest predicted risk (based on literature). By Month 4 (2027-02-13), gate decision: if top 5 pass, expand testing to remaining 5–10. If any of top 5 fail, reformulate and delay Cluster 1 lock to Month 9 (2027-07-13). Avoids spending USD 100–200k on testing analytes that may be removed for other reasons.
  • Shift to synthetic binders if cross-reactivity is pervasive: if >30% of antibody pairs fail due to cross-binding by Month 5 (2027-03-13), pivot to aptamers or engineered-protein binders (higher specificity, lower cross-reactivity risk, but less validation history). Requires USD 300–500k and 8–12 week delay, but may unlock otherwise intractable multiplex analyte sets. Trade timeline (slip Cluster 1 lock to Month 10–12 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-10-13) for technical feasibility.

Create Document 6: Unit Economics and Payer Reimbursement Validation

ID: ce121c7e-d2a6-4641-acd1-7687cbf910d6

Description: Bottom-up COGS model for Cluster 1 at 1k, 10k, and 50k cartridges/month; payer willingness-to-pay survey (10-15 labs, clinicians, payers); CPT coding strategy (unbundled, bundled, or per-cartridge modular codes); health-economic analysis (cost per diagnosis, cost-effectiveness vs. standard-of-care); and three net-revenue scenarios (low USD 50-100, base USD 100-150, high USD 150-200 per run). Identifies reimbursement ceiling, margin target (>=40-50% at realistic volumes), and triggers for design retreat if cost exceeds ceiling. Primary audience: CFO, product officer, board. Validates whether USD 25 COGS ceiling and USD 100-200 revenue assumption are achievable.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Financial Officer and Chief Product Officer (with payer strategist and health-economics consultant)

Primary Template: Medical-device unit economics model; payer coverage analysis template

Secondary Template: Health-economics analysis model (cost-effectiveness, budget-impact); CPT coding petition checklist

Steps to Create:

  • Build bottom-up COGS: cartridge body, bonded fluidic layers, reagents, QC consumables, packaging, overhead allocation at 1k, 10k, 50k volume. Lock USD 25/cartridge ceiling by Month 6 (2027-04-13); design-gate exit if COGS exceeds ceiling.
  • Survey 10-15 labs, clinicians, health systems, payers on willingness-to-pay for a 50-analyte panel; document three price-point scenarios (USD 100, 150, 200 per run).
  • Model gross margin at each price and volume; calculate breakeven volume.
  • Develop CPT coding strategy: consult AMA RUC or CPT advisor on code options (unbundled per-analyte, single bundled code, modular per-cartridge); estimate payer reimbursement and discounts for each pathway.
  • Commission preliminary health-economics analysis: cost per diagnosis, cost-effectiveness vs. reference standard, impact on downstream testing cost, patient outcomes if available.
  • By Month 6 (2027-04-13), initiate payer discussions (3-5 major plans); by Month 9 (2027-07-13), lock realistic net-revenue assumption (low, mid, high case).
  • If base-case margin projects <40% at 50k/month, recommend design retreat: narrow analyte menu or reformat to higher-margin lower-complexity panel.

Approval Authorities: Chief Financial Officer, Chief Product Officer, Board of Directors

Essential Information:

  • Define Unit Economics Model: Bottom-up COGS for Cluster 1 cartridge (10–15 analytes) at pilot (1k), mid (10k), and scale (50k) volumes; itemize cartridge body (USD 2–4), bonded fluidics (USD 1–2), reagents (USD 4–8), QC consumables (USD 2–4), packaging (USD 2–3), allocation overhead.
  • Establish COGS Ceiling and Margin Target: Lock USD 25/cartridge ceiling by Month 6 (2027-04-13); model gross margin >=60% at 50k/month volume; identify design trade-offs (analyte count, integration depth, reagent complexity) if COGS exceeds ceiling.
  • Quantify Net Revenue per Run: Conduct willingness-to-pay survey (10–15 labs, clinicians, payers); document three scenarios (low USD 50–100, base USD 100–150, high USD 150–200 per run); identify realistic payer reimbursement ceiling.
  • Model CPT Coding Strategy: Define unbundled (per-analyte codes), bundled (single code for 50 analytes), or modular (per-cartridge) coding pathways; estimate payer reimbursement and discounts for each; identify CPT petition process and timeline if new code required.
  • Conduct Payer Coverage Landscape Analysis: For top 20 analytes in Cluster 1, identify existing CPT codes, reimbursement rates, and payer policies; by Month 6 (2027-04-13), initiate discussions with 2–3 major payers (Medicare, Aetna, Anthem) on multi-analyte bundle coverage.
  • Commission Health-Economics Analysis: Calculate cost per diagnosis, cost-effectiveness vs. standard-of-care reference panel, budget impact on health system, downstream testing savings if measured; present evidence for payer value propositions.
  • Develop Three Revenue Scenarios: Model cumulative 60-month revenue (Months 0–60 = 2026-10-13 to 2031-10-13) for low (USD 50–100), base (USD 100–150), and high (USD 150–200) per-run net revenue; include volume ramp (10k/month Month 36 = 2029-10-13, 50k/month Month 48 = 2030-10-13).
  • Identify Breakeven Volume: Calculate fixed cost baseline (annual burn USD 3.75–7.5M estimate); determine cartridges/month and revenue/month needed for operational breakeven; compare to market demand assumptions.
  • Test Design-Retreat Triggers: If modeled gross margin at base-case revenue (USD 100–150) and 50k/month volume falls below 40% due to COGS, recommend design options: narrow Cluster 1 to 5–8 highest-value analytes, or simplify cartridge architecture (reduce integration depth, lower reagent count).
  • Create Executive Summary for Board: Present COGS ceiling (USD 25), margin target (>=60%), realistic net revenue (USD 100–150), breakeven volume (~2–11k cartridges/month estimate), and three scenario outcomes (upside if premium reimbursement, downside if bundled at USD 100); flag margin risk if multi-cartridge menu is priced per panel rather than per-cartridge.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate COGS model overstates profitability; at Month 18 (2028-04-13), pilot-scale manufacturing discovers actual cost is USD 35–45/cartridge instead of modeled USD 15–25, requiring 3–6 month design-for-cost sprint and USD 200–500k rework, or triggering unplanned margin compression.
  • Payer coverage not validated; assuming USD 200/run reimbursement, discovering at launch (Month 48 = 2030-10-13) that payers cover only highest-value analytes at USD 50–100 reduces net revenue 50–75%, requiring either price cuts that breach COGS targets or sales-volume increases of 3–5× (USD 5–10M unplanned marketing).
  • CPT coding strategy mismatch; if bundled coding not available, company must bill per analyte (500 separate codes), creating administrative burden and payer resistance; alternatively, unbundled coding at USD 20–30 per analyte yields <USD 50–100 per-run panel revenue, making unit economics unviable.
  • Unit-economics gate missing; discovering at Month 24 (2028-10-13) that gross margin is 20–30% instead of 60% target forces design retreat or revenue model pivot without time to redesign; USD 2–5M in development capital becomes stranded.
  • Multi-cartridge menu economics opaque; if Cluster 1 (50 analytes = 4–5 cartridges) costs USD 160–225 in COGS but payers reimburse only USD 100–150 per panel, margin is negative to 20%, making the modular strategy economically indefensible.
  • Breakeven volume not compared to market demand; projecting breakeven at 2k–11k cartridges/month without evidence that real-world adoption reaches that volume risks building capacity for demand that never materializes, stranding USD 2–4M in Newark capital.

Worst Case Scenario: The company locks a USD 25/cartridge COGS ceiling based on incomplete design, then discovers at pilot scale (Month 12 = 2027-10-13) that realistic cost is USD 35–45 due to reagent complexity, tooling yield loss, or unforeseen bonding defects. Simultaneously, payer discussions (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-07-13) reveal that bundled reimbursement is unavailable and per-analyte coding yields only USD 50–100 per 50-analyte run (1/2 the base-case assumption). Gross margin drops to 10–30% instead of 60% target. The company must choose: redesign cartridge (3–6 month delay, USD 200–500k cost), narrow Cluster 1 from 50 to 20 analytes (reducing clinical value and market appeal), or accept 10–30% margin and delay profitability 3–5 years. Series A investors, unaware of unit-economics uncertainty until Month 12 (2027-10-13), demand corrective action. Cost-of-goods redesign adds 6 months to design freeze, pushing FDA submission from Month 30 (2029-04-13) to Month 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13) and clearance to Month 42–54 (2030-04-13 to 2031-04-13). Newark build-out capital (USD 2–3M released at Month 18 = 2028-04-13) now purchases equipment for a narrower-margin product, reducing long-term return-on-investment and potentially triggering additional capital raises at 30–50% valuation discount (USD 10–15M dilution). Investor confidence erodes; Series B fundraising at Month 24 (2028-10-13) is difficult, requiring 18–24 month longer timeline to profitability.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 6 (2027-04-13), the unit-economics model is complete, validated with 15 payers and 10 clinical sites, and shows: COGS ceiling of USD 25/cartridge is achievable at 10k/month volume through targeted design choices (high-sensitivity immunoassay, optimized bonding, reagent lot-size efficiency). Payers signal USD 150–200 reimbursement per 50-analyte panel based on early health-economics evidence showing 30–40% reduction in follow-up testing vs. standard-of-care, yielding gross margin of 60–75% at 50k/month scale. Market research confirms willingness-to-adopt among 500+ clinical sites and 50+ hospital systems for a 50-analyte initial menu. Design-retreat triggers are defined with board approval; if COGS exceeds USD 27 or margin falls below 50%, Cluster 1 is narrowed to 30 highest-value analytes, preserving viability. Payer coverage applications are pre-drafted for the top 15 analytes, enabling rapid post-clearance reimbursement negotiation. Series A investors gain confidence in unit economics; capital release at Month 12 (2027-10-13) and Month 18 (2028-04-13) gates is approved in full (USD 2–3M per tranche), enabling Newark fit-out, clinical-study completion, and FDA submission on schedule. At Month 30 (2029-04-13), the 510(k) submission includes health-economic and CPT-coding evidence that accelerates FDA review to 4–6 months, with clearance by Month 36 (2029-10-13). First commercial cartridges ship by Month 48 (2030-10-13); with validated unit economics and payer coverage, adoption ramps to 8k cartridges/month by Month 60 (2031-10-13), generating USD 12–16M annual revenue and a clear path to Series B and profitability.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If internal COGS modeling is insufficient by Month 3 (2027-01-13), contract a medical-device cost-engineering firm (estimated USD 50–100k) to conduct independent bottom-up COGS analysis using actual component quotes, supplier data, and yield assumptions; lock ceiling by Month 6 (2027-04-13) based on third-party analysis rather than internal estimates.
  • If payer interviews (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-07-13) suggest reimbursement is <USD 100 per panel, immediately pivot to a 'high-value analyte' strategy: model revenue with only the top 5–10 analytes (lipids, glucose, kidney markers, liver enzymes) bundled at USD 50–80, and offer additional analytes as unbundled add-ons at USD 5–10 each; recalculate breakeven volume and margin; communicate revised business model to investors by Month 12 (2027-10-13).
  • If CPT coding landscape analysis (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-04-13) indicates that bundled CPT codes for multiplex panels are unavailable or have low reimbursement, file a CPT-code petition with the AMA RUC (Relative Value Scale Update Committee) by Month 9 (2027-07-13), requesting a new 'multiplex cardiovascular panel' or 'comprehensive metabolic plus' code; alternatively, use existing 'panels' (CPT 80053 = comprehensive metabolic panel at ~USD 40–50 reimbursement) as an interim billing strategy and negotiate a supplementary CPT 99000 handling/processing code for the modular cartridge approach.
  • If health-economics analysis (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-07-13) fails to demonstrate cost-effectiveness (cost per diagnosis not lower than standard-of-care panel), delay the health-economics submission to payers and instead focus on regulatory evidence (analytical accuracy, clinical concordance) for clearance; use real-world post-launch evidence (time-to-result, testing convenience, physician workflow improvement) to justify premium pricing after clearance, when market pressure is lower.
  • If breakeven-volume analysis (Month 4 = 2027-02-13) reveals that the company needs 5k–10k cartridges/month to cover USD 3.75–7.5M/year burn (estimated), and market demand is uncertain, establish a narrower beachhead customer (e.g., one 500-bed health system, or 3–5 major reference labs) with a multi-year contract guaranteeing minimum volumes of 2k–5k cartridges/month; use contract-backed capacity commitment to justify Newark investment and validate demand.
  • If unit-economics modeling is incomplete by Month 12 (2027-10-13) due to design uncertainty or supplier data gaps, defer the Month 12 (2027-10-13) analytical feasibility gate decision by 4–6 weeks and conduct a 'COGS proof-of-concept' pilot: manufacture 2,000–5,000 cartridges at a contract molding and filling facility at pilot scale, measure actual cost, yield, and shelf-life, and use real-world data to validate or revise the unit-economics model; this adds USD 50–100k and 4–6 weeks but provides ground-truth cost data instead of modeling assumptions.
  • If margin targets (>=60%) appear unachievable with a 50-analyte Cluster 1, immediately develop a 'lower-complexity' fallback menu: reduce Cluster 1 from 50 to 15–20 analytes focused only on the highest-clinical-value tests (e.g., cardiovascular: lipid panel + hs-CRP + troponin); model COGS for this narrower menu (estimated USD 12–18/cartridge), achieve 70–80% gross margin, and use the simpler product as Phase 1 launch; expand to a 50–100 analyte menu only after Phase 1 generates revenue and Cluster 2 COGS validation.
  • If payer discussions (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-07-13) stall or result in 'wait-and-see' responses, proactively establish a direct-to-consumer or employer-wellness revenue stream: negotiate contracts with 3–5 large employers or employee-assistance providers to offer the multiplex panel at USD 50–100 per employee per year (self-pay or employer-subsidized), bypassing payer approval; generate USD 100–500k/year in parallel revenue and real-world outcome data, then use employer satisfaction to negotiate payer coverage.
  • If multi-cartridge menu economics (4–5 cartridges for 50 analytes costing USD 160–225 COGS but reimbursed as a USD 100–150 panel) remain unviable, restructure the product as a 'tiered menu': Tier 1 is a 10–15 analyte 'quick screen' cartridge at USD 40–50 reimbursement (high margin, broad use); Tier 2 is an expanded 30–40 analyte 'comprehensive' cartridge at USD 80–120 (mid margin, specialist use); bundle pricing and billing so customers choose Tier 1 or Tier 2, not both; this simplifies inventory and improves economics.

  • Detail the pilot-fill plan for Month 9 (2027-07-13): who runs it (Phase 1 in-house, contract manufacturer, or shared facility), equipment, process parameters, yield measurement criteria (target ≥85%; gate threshold ≥80% at lower 95% CI), first-pass defect tracking, data collection and analysis.
  • Establish equipment procurement and lead-time timeline: request quotes from filling-equipment, molding, and reagent-dispensing vendors by Month 3 (2027-01-13); identify long-lead items (>6 months: characterize and lock by Month 12 = 2027-10-13 for possible expediting if gate passes); issue binding orders only at Month 18 (2028-04-13) release.
