  • Specify Phase 2 (released Month 18 = 2028-04-13 upon design freeze and pilot yield ≥85%) facility scope: additional 1,000–1,500 sq ft, full automated or semi-automated cartridge-filling line (target throughput 10,000+ cartridges/month), reagent-dispensing automation, quality-control throughput, scaling to 50,000 cartridges/month capacity.
  • Define contract-manufacturer qualification criteria and process: identify ≥2 injection molders and assembly partners by Month 4 (2027-02-13); design-for-manufacturability (DFM) review and 90-day concurrent engineering partnership by Month 6 (2027-04-13); first-article run (1,000–5,000 cartridges) by Month 9 (2027-07-13); quality agreement specifying defect rate <5%, first-pass yield >90%, price locks, lead times.
  • Quantify capital expenditures with timing and contingencies: Phase 1 USD 500–800k (Months 3–6 = 2027-01-13 to 2027-04-13); Phase 2 USD 2–3M filling-line capital + USD 400–600k equipment contingency (released Month 18 = 2028-04-13; deployment Months 24–30 = 2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13); total Newark capex USD 2.9–4.4M; identify funding source (program equity vs. supplier financing).
  • Establish gate-linked capital-release decision rule: Month 12 (2027-10-13) analytical feasibility gate triggers Phase 2 release only if yield ≥85% (≥5 batches x 1,000; lower 95% CI ≥80%), lot CV <10%, shelf-life ≥12 months projected. If gate fails, conduct 4-week design review; if unresolved by Month 15 (2028-01-13), activate Fallback V1 and pause Newark full build-out.
  • Detail long-lead-item contingency planning: specify which items have 6–12 month lead times; set cancellable-deposit threshold (cancellable after Month 12 = 2027-10-13 gate passes); establish supplier agreements including force-majeure and delay-penalty clauses; maintain 20% equipment-cost contingency (USD 400–600k).
  • Define supplier qualification, quality-agreement and dual-sourcing strategy: lock agreements for contract molders by Month 6 (2027-04-13); establish quality requirements (defect rate, first-pass yield, delivery lead-time, price-lock period); maintain monthly supplier scorecard (defect rate, on-time delivery, cost); activate backup supplier within 2 weeks if primary defect rate exceeds 10%.
  • Specify compliance and facility standards: BSL-2 biosafety capability, ISO 13485 and 21 CFR 820 design controls and quality-system readiness by Month 18 (2028-04-13), utilities (power, water, HVAC for temperature and humidity control), waste-handling (medical/biohazard permits), environmental monitoring and clean-room certification.
  • Establish staffing and operational readiness: identify operations lead and manufacturing engineering leadership by Month 1 (2026-11-13); define process technician, quality-control, and maintenance staffing for Phase 1 (2–4 FTE estimated) and Phase 2 (4–6 FTE); training and validation timeline for GMP-equivalent operations by Month 15 (2028-01-13).
  • Develop production-readiness and scale-up plan: pilot fills yield validation (Month 9 = 2027-07-13); design-freeze and process lock (Month 18 = 2028-04-13); stability-data package for FDA submission (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13); ramp to 10,000 cartridges/month by Month 36 (2029-10-13); operations continuous-improvement (yield, defect, cycle-time).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Vague Phase 1 scope leads to underestimated facility cost (USD 200–300k over budget) and delayed operational readiness (2–4 months); insufficient lab capacity for pilot fills forces use of contract manufacturer, losing process control and increasing cartridge cost by USD 5–10 per unit.
  • Missing or incomplete DFM review delays mold commissioning and pushes pilot-fill start from Month 9 (2027-07-13) to Month 12 (2027-10-13), compressing the time available to meet the Month 12 (2027-10-13) yield gate and risking a failed gate decision.
  • Failure to lock contract-manufacturer agreements and dual-sourcing by Month 6 (2027-04-13) results in late-stage mold delays, tooling re-work (USD 50–150k, 3–4 months) if design changes post-commitment, or supplier capacity gaps that stall fills in Months 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13).
  • Absent or inadequate gate-release decision rule (clear yield, lot CV, shelf-life thresholds) leads to ambiguous Month 12 (2027-10-13) results being interpreted subjectively, delaying or enabling a Phase 2 capital release based on political pressure rather than technical merit, or spending USD 2–3M on a filling line when yield is unproven.
  • Weak or missing supplier quality-agreement language (no defect-rate penalty, no price-lock, no lead-time commitment) results in supplier quality degradation after fit-out (defect rate rises from 5% to 15%+), manufacturing delays, rework costs (USD 100–500k), and cartridge-shelf-life risk.
  • Incomplete or delayed facility-compliance documentation (BSL-2 certification, waste-handling permits, ISO 13485 assessment) discovered at Month 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) forces facility closure, contractor work, or remediation (USD 100–300k, 2–3 months), blocking pilot fills and delaying the Month 12 (2027-10-13) gate.
  • Overestimation of Phase 1 pilot-fill capability (e.g., claiming 10,000 cartridges/month when design is 1,000–5,000) sets unrealistic expectations for clinical-study supply, forces rushed or inadequate stability testing, and exposes the company to FDA scrutiny of the clinical cartridge lot.
  • Missing contingency plan for equipment lead-time slips (supplier bankruptcy, shipping delays, custom-equipment re-design) causes filling-line deployment to slip from Months 24–30 (2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13) to Months 30–36 (2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13), coinciding with FDA pre-approval inspection and manufacturing-readiness demonstration, creating a critical-path bottleneck.
  • Lack of phased release discipline (early commitment to Phase 2 capital before analytical feasibility gate passes) commits USD 2–3M to equipment ordering before the design is proven manufacturable, stranding capital if yield falls short and requires design re-work.

Worst Case Scenario: Failure to execute a disciplined, gate-linked Newark phased build-out plan results in one or more of the following cascading failures: (1) Phase 1 facility is leased and fitted but is undersized or lacks critical capabilities (stability chambers, QC instrumentation), forcing reliance on contract manufacturers who charge USD 5–10 per cartridge for pilot fills and lack process-design partnership. (2) Pilot fills are delayed to Month 12 (2027-10-13) or later, leaving insufficient time to achieve the Month 12 (2027-10-13) yield gate and forcing a gate delay or miss. (3) Contract molders are not qualified early, tooling is delayed, or mold changes are discovered too late, adding USD 50–150k in re-work and 3–4 months of delay. (4) Phase 2 capital of USD 2–3M is committed to equipment orders before the Month 12 (2027-10-13) yield gate passes, and when yield falls to 70–80% (triggering a design review), the filling-line equipment is partially ordered and non-cancellable, stranding USD 1–2M. (5) Filling-line deployment is delayed to Months 30–36 (2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13), coinciding with FDA pre-approval inspection, manufacturing-readiness audit, and clinical-study close-out, exposing the company to FDA 483 citations for immature manufacturing processes, unvalidated filling lines, and insufficient lot-testing data. (6) Cumulative capex overruns (facility cost +20–30%, equipment cost +30–50%, contingency exhausted) push total Newark cost to USD 4–5M+ (20–36% over budget estimate), requiring Series B upsizing by USD 1–2M and increased dilution. The combination of manufacturing delays, regulatory findings and capex overruns delays FDA clearance by 6–12 months (to Months 42–54 = 2030-04-13 to 2031-04-13), blocks first commercial sales until Months 54–66 (2031-04-13 to 2032-04-13), and increases cumulative burn to USD 30–45M, forcing extended Series B/C fundraising at unfavorable valuations. Probability of this scenario: 15–25% if the plan lacks clear gate discipline and early DFM engagement.

Best Case Scenario: A disciplined, fully detailed Newark phased build-out plan with clear gate-linked capital release, early DFM engagement and supplier qualification enables the following positive outcomes: (1) Phase 1 facility is leased by Month 3 (2027-01-13) and operational by Month 6 (2027-04-13), with integrated reagent formulation, pilot filling and lot-release capability. Pilot fills are conducted internally or under close partnership with a contract molder by Month 9 (2027-07-13), yielding 1,000–5,000 cartridges and immediate process data. (2) The Month 12 (2027-10-13) analytical feasibility gate is met with >85% yield, <10% lot CV and ≥12 month shelf-life projection, enabling a disciplined board vote on Phase 2 capital release. (3) Contract molders are dual-qualified by Month 6 (2027-04-13), DFM review is concurrent, first-article runs validate tolerances by Month 9 (2027-07-13), and mold tooling is placed on a long-lead order (with cancellable deposit) by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Binding equipment orders are issued only at Month 18 (2028-04-13) after design freeze, reducing the risk of obsolete tooling or process re-work. (4) Phase 2 filling-line fit-out begins Month 18 (2028-04-13) and is operational by Months 24–30 (2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13), with FDA pre-approval inspection conducted Month 28–30 (2029-02-13 to 2029-04-13) finding a mature, validated manufacturing process. (5) Cumulative Newark capex remains within budget (USD 2.9–4.4M), with no major overruns, and the filling line is ready to scale to 10,000 cartridges/month by Month 36 (2029-10-13) in support of FDA submission and post-clearance demand. (6) The clear gate discipline and early supplier engagement reduce manufacturing-readiness risk, enable FDA clearance by Months 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13), and allow first commercial sales by Month 48 (2030-10-13) without delays. The well-documented, validated Newark process becomes a competitive advantage and supports Series B investor confidence. Cumulative burn remains within the USD 15–30M range (estimate), and post-clearance scaling becomes a straightforward manufacturing optimization. Probability of this scenario: 40–50% with disciplined execution and early stakeholder alignment.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Defer Phase 1 facility investment entirely until Month 12 (2027-10-13) analytical feasibility gate passes. Use a contract-research or contract-manufacturing facility (e.g., shared lab space in Fremont, Hayward, or a CRO) for reagent formulation, pilot fills, and stability testing in Months 3–12 (2027-01-13 to 2027-10-13). Cost: USD 200–300k (higher per-cartridge fill cost, USD 3–5 per unit for pilot fills, estimated USD 20–50k total over 1,000–5,000 cartridges). Advantage: preserves cash and flexibility; Phase 2 facility is leased and equipped only after yield is proven. Disadvantage: loss of process control, vendor dependence, and less intimate partnership with the fill-line design. Timeline: same (Phase 1 facility still operational by Month 6 = 2027-04-13 for production prep, if gate passes).
  • Implement a phased release of Phase 2 capital with intermediate-stage gates (Month 15 = 2028-01-13 gates in addition to Month 12 = 2027-10-13). Tranche 2a (Month 12 = 2027-10-13, USD 500–800k): order long-lead equipment (filling machine, reagent dispensers) with cancellable deposits; design the filling-line space (layout, utilities). Tranche 2b (Month 18 = 2028-04-13, USD 1.5–2M): issue binding equipment orders and begin facility fit-out only if design freeze is locked and intermediate pilot results confirm yield and shelf-life targets. Advantage: further granularity and flexibility; capital commitment is smaller and more phased. Disadvantage: extends decision cycles and may delay equipment delivery if funding decisions are made sequentially.
  • Outsource the entire Newark filling operation to an established contract manufacturer with GMP and ISO 13485 capabilities (e.g., a medical-device CDMO in California or nationally). Newark facility focus shifts to reagent formulation and lot-release QC only (Phase 1 scope). Advantage: eliminates capital spend on filling equipment (USD 2–3M savings), transfers manufacturing risk and compliance burden to the CDMO, and may accelerate fill timelines if the CDMO has excess capacity. Disadvantage: loss of vertical control, higher per-unit variable cost (USD 5–8 per cartridge fill, vs. USD 3–4 in-house estimated), dependency on CDMO capacity and quality, and reduced IP ownership of manufacturing process. Timeline: Phase 1 (reagent lab) still leads; filling is contracted from Month 9 (2027-07-13) onward.
  • Conduct a comprehensive Design-for-Manufacturability (DFM) feasibility study with ≥3 contract molders and filling-equipment vendors by Month 4 (2027-02-13) (accelerated DFM, ahead of the proposed Month 6 = 2027-04-13 target). Use the DFM findings to make a 'build vs. outsource' decision by Month 6 (2027-04-13): if molders report that the cartridge design has <70% expected first-pass yield or requires >USD 35 COGS at scale, immediately pivot to full outsourcing or a narrower Fallback V1 cartridge (10 vs. 15 analytes). Advantage: discovers manufacturability issues early (3–4 months earlier), enables a course correction before Phase 1 capital is spent. Disadvantage: requires intensive vendor engagement early and may pressure vendors to provide preliminary data with low confidence; decision might be premature if design is still evolving.
  • Establish a joint venture or contract-manufacturing partnership with an established IVD CDMO or incumbent diagnostics firm (e.g., Roche subsidiary, Siemens Healthcare, or a dedicated CDMO such as Catalent, Alcami, or Viant) to operate the Newark facility. The startup retains ownership of the cartridge design and IP; the partner operates the cleanroom, quality system, and manufacturing under a fee-per-cartridge or milestone-based arrangement. Advantage: transfers capital and operational risk; the partner brings existing ISO 13485 certifications, FDA experience, and manufacturing efficiency; the startup avoids the distraction of facility management. Disadvantage: reduced direct control, margin compression (CDMO fees typically 15–25% of product cost), and IP/relationship dependency; the partner may impose minimum volume commitments or exclusivity restrictions.
  • Compress Phase 1 and Phase 2 into a single accelerated Phase 1+ by Month 9 (2027-07-13): lease a larger facility (4,000–5,000 sq ft) and fit out both reagent formulation and a prototype filling line in parallel (Months 3–9 = 2027-01-13 to 2027-07-13). Conduct pilot fills by Month 9 (2027-07-13) at the accelerated timeline. Advantage: avoids a second lease and fit-out cycle; faster learning cycle; potential to meet the Month 12 (2027-10-13) gate with more mature fill-process data. Disadvantage: higher upfront capex (USD 800k–1.2M for Phase 1+, vs. USD 500–800k phased); risk of over-investing before the yield gate passes; requires concurrent design-freeze work (Months 3–9 = 2027-01-13 to 2027-07-13) to finalize fill parameters, which may not align with analytical-feasibility work.
  • Adopt a 'minimum viable manufacturing' strategy: Phase 1 focuses only on reagent formulation and lot-release QC (micro-batch manual fills for clinical-study cartridges, 100–500 units at a time). Contract all production-scale filling to external partners until post-FDA-clearance. Newark facility cost: USD 300–500k (smaller space, minimal equipment). Advantage: lowest capital commitment; preserves cash for clinical studies and regulatory work. Disadvantage: no internal learning on cartridge filling at scale; external dependence for clinical-study supply and commercial fills; loss of competitive leverage if the CDMO controls the fill process.

Create Document 8: Quality Management System (QMS) and Design Control Charter

ID: d43a2346-b8fb-4a92-9967-400d057380c8

Description: Formal establishment of ISO 13485 quality system, design controls (21 CFR 820.30), and design history file (DHF) governance from Month 0 (2026-10-13). Documents design-input and design-output procedures, design-review schedule (monthly), change-control process (all design changes after Month 5 = 2027-03-13 require written justification, risk assessment, quality sign-off), risk-management (ISO 14971) integration, and DHF archival and version control. Specifies roles (quality director authority over design changes), approval gates, and FDA inspection readiness timeline (internal audit Month 6 = 2027-04-13, certification Month 18 = 2028-04-13, mock inspection Months 28-30 = 2029-02-13 to 2029-04-13). Primary audience: quality lead, R&D, board. Prevents design-control gaps that trigger FDA 483 observations and clearance delays.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Quality Officer / Regulatory Affairs Lead

Primary Template: ISO 13485 design controls SOP; FDA 21 CFR 820.30 design-control guidance

Secondary Template: Design history file (DHF) template; change-control and risk-management procedure

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 2 (2026-12-13), establish written Design Control Charter: all design decisions from Month 0 (2026-10-13) documented with design inputs, design outputs, design reviews, risk assessments, and verification.
  • Designate design-control owner (quality director) with authority to approve/reject design changes.
  • Implement electronic DHF repository with version control, access logs, and audit trails compliant with 21 CFR 11.
  • Establish monthly design-review meeting cadence (CTO, quality lead, R&D director, regulatory consultant); document all discussions.
  • Define change-control process: changes after Month 5 (2027-03-13) require written change request, design verification, risk reassessment, and quality/CTO sign-off before implementation.
  • Conduct internal ISO 13485 audit by Month 6 (2027-04-13); close major gaps within 4 weeks.
  • Engage ISO 13485 accredited registrar by Month 15 (2028-01-13); schedule certification audit for Month 18 (2028-04-13).
  • Schedule mock FDA inspection (simulated by external consultant) at Months 28-30 (2029-02-13 to 2029-04-13); close all observations before pre-approval inspection.

Approval Authorities: Chief Quality Officer, CEO, ISO 13485 Accredited Registrar (for certification)

Essential Information:

  • Define and document the Quality Management System (QMS) charter aligned with ISO 13485 and 21 CFR 820.30, establishing design-control procedures, design-history file (DHF) governance, and approval authorities from Month 0 (2026-10-13).
  • Specify design-input requirements (including analyte-performance criteria: concordance ≥95%, CV <10%), design-output specifications, design-review meeting cadence (monthly minimum), and design-verification methods for each analyte cluster.
  • Establish written change-control process governing design modifications after Month 5 (2027-03-13): all changes require written justification, risk assessment per ISO 14971, quality sign-off, and documented traceability to DHF.
  • Define role assignments: quality director authority over design changes, CTO/R&D director responsibility for technical content, CEO/board authority for gate decisions and capital release tied to quality milestones.
  • Detail DHF repository requirements: electronic system with version control, audit trails per 21 CFR Part 11, access logs, document retrieval time <1 hour for FDA inspection.
  • Specify design-review documentation requirements: attendance, action items, risk-assessment updates, approval signatures, and closure evidence for each monthly meeting through design freeze (Month 18 = 2028-04-13).
  • Establish internal ISO 13485 audit plan: baseline audit by Month 6 (2027-04-13), gap-closure protocol (major findings closed <4 weeks), and corrective-action tracking.
  • Define ISO 13485 certification timeline: registrar engagement by Month 15 (2028-01-13), certification audit Month 18 (2028-04-13), certificate issuance target <4 weeks post-audit.
  • Schedule mock FDA inspection (external consultant) at Months 28-30 (2029-02-13 to 2029-04-13); specify inspection scope (design controls, complaint handling, DHF completeness, traceability), observation response protocol (root-cause analysis, corrective action), and closure timeline (<4 weeks).
  • Document risk-management integration: ISO 14971 risk register updated monthly, risk controls verified post-design freeze, residual-risk assessment for each analyte cluster, risk mitigations tied to analytical-feasibility gates (Month 12 = 2027-10-13, Month 18 = 2028-04-13).
  • Define traceability matrix: design inputs to outputs, risk controls to design features, design changes to risk reassessments, analytical performance data to DHF records.
  • Establish complaint-handling and nonconformance-tracking procedures: feedback loop from clinical studies, failed analytes, yield shortfalls to design-review meetings and change-control process.
  • Specify training and qualification requirements: all personnel involved in design decisions trained on design controls, change control, risk management; training records maintained in quality system.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or missing design-control documentation triggers FDA 483 observations during pre-approval inspection (Month 36-42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13), delaying clearance 2-4 months and requiring costly remediation.
  • Inadequate design-input specification (missing analyte-performance thresholds) allows ambiguous design outputs; analytes fail concordance gates late in development, forcing redesign and 3-6 month delays post-Month 12 (2027-10-13).
  • Weak change-control process permits undocumented design modifications after Month 5 (2027-03-13); untraced changes invalidate risk assessments and design verification, creating regulatory non-compliance and FDA refusal to clear.
  • Absent DHF or poor repository management (paper files, lost records, version confusion) makes device history unrecoverable; FDA inspection reveals control gaps, triggering warning letter or product recall risk.
  • Missing ISO 14971 risk documentation and controls leaves design vulnerabilities unidentified; safety/performance failures emerge post-launch, exposing company to product liability and regulatory action.
  • Late or incomplete QMS build-out discovered at Month 18-24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13) requires emergency quality hiring and system redesign, consuming USD 300-500k and 3-6 months parallel to clinical studies.
  • Lack of traceability between design inputs, outputs, risk controls and analytical-gate results prevents FDA from verifying design adequacy; submission is rejected and resubmission adds 6-12 months.
  • Inadequate design-review documentation (no meeting notes, unsigned approval) allows disputes over design decisions; gate approval vote is challenged post-facto, delaying capital release and design freeze.
  • Missing complaint-handling and nonconformance procedures prevent early identification of analyte-failure patterns; failures accumulate silently and are discovered only during clinical studies, invalidating whole clusters and forcing retreat.

Worst Case Scenario: The company completes Cluster 1 development and clinical studies (by Month 24 = 2028-10-13) but has no formal design-control or QMS documentation. During FDA pre-approval inspection (Month 36-42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13), inspectors find missing DHF, no design-input/output traceability, undocumented design changes, absent risk assessments, and complaint records scattered across email. FDA issues a Warning Letter and refuses to clear the device. Remediation requires hiring a quality consultant (USD 200-400k), rebuilding the entire QMS retroactively (4-6 months), re-conducting design verification for all changed elements, and re-submitting to FDA. Clearance is delayed 12-18 months, pushing launch from Month 48 (2030-10-13) to Month 60-66 (2031-10-13 to 2032-04-13). Series C fundraising is jeopardized; investor confidence collapses 40-50%. Newark facility remains under-utilized, burning USD 150-200k/year in idle overhead. The company loses first-mover advantage; competitors launch similar products and capture 30-50% of market share. Cumulative financial impact: USD 1-2 million in remediation, USD 2-3 million in delayed revenue, and 50-60% valuation dilution in Series C.

Best Case Scenario: Quality-management system and design controls are established formally by Month 2 (2026-12-13), with electronic DHF live, monthly design-review meetings documented, and a quality director empowered to enforce change control. All design decisions from Month 0 (2026-10-13) are retrospectively captured in the DHF by Month 3 (2027-01-13). Monthly design reviews identify analyte-performance gaps early (Month 4-6 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-04-13); underperforming analytes are redesigned or retired before the analytical-feasibility gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-13), preventing wasted clinical-study effort. Design freeze is executed cleanly at Month 18 (2028-04-13) with complete design outputs, risk assessments, and verification evidence. ISO 13485 certification is obtained on schedule at Month 18 (2028-04-13). Mock FDA inspection at Months 28-30 (2029-02-13 to 2029-04-13) identifies only minor documentation gaps, closed within 2 weeks. FDA pre-approval inspection (Month 36-42 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13) is clean; no 483 observations. Device is cleared by Month 42 (2030-04-13). Clinical team, regulatory consultants and investors view the company as disciplined and credible; Series B fundraising is oversubscribed. Newark fills first commercial cartridges by Month 45 (2030-07-13), first sales by Month 48 (2030-10-13). Design-control discipline enables rapid Cluster 2 validation and 510(k) submission by Month 42 (2030-04-13), clearing by Month 48-54 (2030-10-13 to 2031-04-13). The 500-analyte cumulative menu achieves credibility and market traction faster than competitors. Impact: 6-12 month timeline acceleration, USD 200-500k in remediation costs avoided, Series B valuation premium 20-30%, time-to-profitability reduced by 18-24 months.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage a quality-systems consultant experienced in FDA device submissions (USD 150-250k over Months 1-18 = 2026-11-13 to 2028-04-13) to lead QMS and design-control implementation. Consultant drafts procedures, trains personnel, and conducts monthly audits. Company executes; consultant validates. Reduces internal quality-staff burden and accelerates certification.
  • Adopt a pre-built ISO 13485 design-control template from an industry body (e.g., RAPS, AAMI, or FDA guidance) and customize for the company's product. Reduces documentation work by 30-40% compared to writing from scratch, but requires careful template evaluation to ensure fit.
  • Hire an interim Chief Quality Officer (CQO) on a fractional or contract basis (20-40 hours/week) from Month 1 (2026-11-13) through Month 18 (2028-04-13) to establish QMS while the permanent CQO is recruited. Reduces permanent-salary burden (USD 30-50k vs USD 150-200k/year) while ensuring expert leadership during critical design phase.
  • Use electronic quality-management software (eMDCM, MasterControl, Veeva, or equivalent; USD 10-20k/year) to automate DHF repository, change control, document version management, and audit trails. Software tracks compliance automatically and reduces manual QMS maintenance, freeing quality staff to focus on design reviews and risk assessment.
  • Defer full ISO 13485 certification to Month 24 (2028-10-13) and instead conduct an internal assessment against the standard at Month 18 (2028-04-13), fix major gaps, and pursue certification immediately before FDA pre-approval inspection (Month 28-36 = 2029-02-13 to 2029-10-13). Reduces certification cost (USD 10-20k vs USD 30-50k if done earlier) but increases risk of late discovery of gaps; suitable only if internal resources are confident and no FDA submissions are planned before Month 18 (2028-04-13).
  • Form a cross-functional Design Review Board (CTO, assay lead, manufacturing/process engineer, quality director, regulatory consultant) that meets bi-weekly instead of monthly to accelerate design decisions and reduce design-cycle time by 20-30%, provided decision documentation is rigorous. Suitable if design velocity is the limiting timeline factor.
  • Conduct the mock FDA inspection earlier (Month 20-24 = 2028-08-13 to 2028-10-13 instead of Months 28-30 = 2029-02-13 to 2029-04-13) to allow more time for gap closure before the real pre-approval inspection. Trade: adds cost (USD 15-20k earlier) and requires more mature QMS documentation, but reduces risk of surprises late in the regulatory timeline.

Create Document 9: Science-First Transparency Charter and External Scientific Advisory Board Governance

ID: 8fbe7927-9355-4e46-b8c7-375f3afaa828

Description: Formal commitment to transparent, published validation and independent scientific oversight. Establishes external scientific advisory board (5-7 members from academia/diagnostics) with quarterly public meetings and audit access to raw data, analyte-removal logs, and failure documentation. Specifies monthly public Analyte Performance Dashboard (pass and fail, with technical details) and Quarterly Transparency Report published on company website. Pre-registers clinical-study protocol on ClinicalTrials.gov before enrollment; publishes results (pass and fail) and Analyte Removal Log with justifications for each excluded assay. Prohibits suppression or selective reporting of weak analytes. Primary audience: board, investors, FDA, payers, clinicians, public. Differentiates against Theranos-era skepticism and builds credibility with regulators and clinicians.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Scientist or Center for Scientific Integrity Lead (with CEO and Communications support)

Primary Template: Scientific advisory board charter and conflict-of-interest policy; transparency and data-sharing agreement template

Secondary Template: ClinicalTrials.gov registration protocol; public dashboard design (Tableau/Looker or custom web)

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 1 (2026-11-13), recruit external scientific advisory board (5-7 members: university chemistry/assay leads, diagnostics-company scientists, clinical-chemistry faculty, independent regulatory consultants).
  • Establish advisory-board charter: quarterly in-person or virtual meetings, audit access to raw data, conflict-of-interest disclosure, publication review and input, data-sharing agreements with IP protections.
  • By Month 2 (2026-12-13), publish a 'Science-First' charter on company website: commit to pre-registered studies, public analyte-level performance reporting, published failures, and no '500 per drop' claims until 3 clusters validated.
  • By Month 3 (2027-01-13), design and launch public Analyte Performance Dashboard: monthly updates showing each analyte's status (validation in progress, pass, fail), accuracy/precision/cross-reactivity summary, shelf-life projection, manufacturing yield.
  • Register clinical-study protocol on ClinicalTrials.gov by Month 10 (2027-08-13); pre-specify analyte-level success criteria and statistical analysis plan.
  • By Month 6 (2027-04-13), publish first Quarterly Transparency Report: validated analytes (Month 6 = 2027-04-13 gate results), any failures, technical root causes, remediation plan.
  • Maintain Analyte Removal Log: for any analyte failing threshold, document failure (e.g., cross-reactivity with interferent X at 5x level), root-cause analysis, reformulation attempt (if any), and final removal justification; publish in quarterly report.

Approval Authorities: Chief Scientist/Integrity Lead, CEO, External Scientific Advisory Board

Essential Information:

  • Define the External Scientific Advisory Board charter: composition (5–7 members from academia, diagnostics, clinical chemistry, independent regulatory); meeting cadence (quarterly public or hybrid); conflict-of-interest disclosure and management; role scope (audit access to raw data, analyte-removal logs, failure documentation, IP-safe data-sharing agreements).
  • Specify the Science-First commitment statement: pledge to pre-register all clinical-study protocols on ClinicalTrials.gov before enrollment; publish analyte-level performance data (accuracy, precision, cross-reactivity, shelf-life, yield) monthly on a public dashboard; publish results of all completed analytes, including failures, in quarterly transparency reports; commit to no '500 per drop' marketing claims until at least 3 analyte clusters are independently validated and peer-reviewed.
  • Design and specify the public Analyte Performance Dashboard: monthly updates showing each analyte in Cluster 1 and beyond—status (in validation, pass, fail), key metrics (concordance %, CV, detection limit, cross-reactivity results, shelf-life projection, manufacturing yield %), root cause of any failure, remediation plan and timeline. Dashboard hosted on company website; updated by 15th of each month.
  • Create the Analyte Removal Log protocol: for any analyte failing a pre-set success threshold (e.g., concordance <95%, CV >10%, cross-reactivity >5% bias at 10× interferent, shelf-life <9 months, yield <80%), document the failure with technical details, investigation results, attempted redesign (if any), and final removal justification. Log published quarterly in transparency report with rationale for each removal.
  • Establish pre-registration discipline: specify that every clinical-study protocol (method-comparison, clinical-validity, biomarker utility) is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov at least 2 weeks before enrollment begins, including pre-specified analyte success criteria, statistical analysis plan, and primary endpoints. Pre-registration is non-negotiable.
  • Define the Quarterly Transparency Report template and cadence: issued at Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24 (2027-01-13, 2027-04-13, 2027-07-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-10-13) minimum; includes summary of validated analytes (with 95% CI accuracy and precision), analytes currently in validation (timeline), analytes that failed (technical cause, no suppression), manufacturing progress (yield, lot CV, shelf-life data), regulatory milestone status (FDA Pre-Sub, ISO 13485, clinical-study enrollment), and forward plan. Published on company website and sent to all investors, advisors, and FDA.
  • Specify governance authority: Chief Scientist or dedicated Center for Scientific Integrity lead owns the charter, dashboard and reports (with CEO and Communications support). Scientific Advisory Board reviews all analyte-performance summaries before publication (within 1 week of posting). Any suppression of data or failure to disclose an analyte failure is grounds for board member resignation and public notification.
  • Define the conflict-of-interest (COI) policy for the Scientific Advisory Board: annual COI disclosure and recusal rules (e.g., if a board member has a competing diagnostics interest, they recuse from that topic); IP protection (advisory-board members sign confidentiality agreements, limiting their ability to exploit company data for competing ventures, with exception carve-outs for pre-existing commitments); publication review (board members may review and comment on company publications before external submission, but do not hold veto; company publishes with board comment summary appended if they choose).
  • Establish analyte-removal criteria and decision process: specified thresholds are locked by Month 2 (2026-12-13) for Cluster 1 (e.g., analytical concordance ≥95%, CV <10%, cross-reactivity ≤5% bias at 10× physiologic interferent, shelf-life ≥9 months at 2–8°C, yield ≥85% at pilot scale). Monthly analyte review meetings (1st Tuesday) assess each analyte against criteria. Any analyte at risk for failure is flagged; redesign or removal decision is made within 4 weeks or it is escalated to the board.
  • Specify the marketing and communications guardrails: no product claim or investor pitch may state '500 tests per drop' or '500 simultaneous analytes' until the company has independently published clinical-study results (peer-reviewed) for at least 3 analyte clusters (50+ analytes total) meeting all concordance and utility thresholds. Until that threshold, marketing language is 'multi-analyte panel,' 'expanding menu,' or 'up to 500 analytes in a growing family of tests.' Internal team communications may refer to the 500-test vision, but all external claims are gated on published evidence.
  • Define the public failure reporting standard: any analyte that fails a threshold, even if a redesign attempt is made, is reported in the next quarterly transparency report with the failure date, metrics, root cause, redesign plan and timeline (if applicable), and final status (removed vs. under redesign). No 'quiet removals' without public disclosure.
  • Establish timeline and approval authorities: Charter adopted and board recruited by Month 2 (2026-12-13); science-first statement published by Month 2 (2026-12-13); first Analyte Performance Dashboard live by Month 3 (2027-01-13) (even if all analytes are still in early validation stage); first Quarterly Transparency Report published by Month 6 (2027-04-13); clinical-study pre-registration on ClinicalTrials.gov by Month 10 (2027-08-13), at least 2 weeks before first-subject enrollment. Ongoing cadence: monthly dashboard updates, quarterly transparency reports. Approval authority: Chief Scientist/Integrity Lead with CEO sign-off and Scientific Advisory Board review.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or absent Scientific Advisory Board charter: without clear composition, conflict-of-interest rules, and data-access scope, the board becomes symbolic rather than functional. Investors and FDA view it as a credibility theater. If a board member has undisclosed competing interests or the company withholds sensitive data, the arrangement collapses publicly, damaging reputation and delaying regulatory review (3–6 month impact). Loss of investor confidence: 15–25% valuation markdown (estimated).
  • No public Analyte Performance Dashboard or vague dashboard design: without a real-time, transparent, metric-level view of each analyte's performance, investors, clinicians and FDA cannot verify the company's claims of progress. Rumors of failed analytes spread through competitors or former employees; the company appears to be hiding results. FDA asks for internal data during Pre-Submission or inspection and discovers analytes failed months earlier but were not disclosed. Regulatory delay: 2–4 months. Investor concern: Series B financing slips 3–6 months.
  • Failure-suppression or selective reporting of analyte performance: if the company removes weak analytes without public disclosure, and this is discovered during FDA inspection or by a board member, the company faces a 483 observation ('failure to transparently report analytical performance'), potential Warning Letter, and regulatory block on submissions. Reputational loss comparable to Theranos (estimated 40–60% valuation impact). Product launch delayed or blocked.
  • Poorly defined analyte-removal criteria or ad-hoc removal decisions: without pre-locked success thresholds (e.g., concordance ≥95%, CV <10%), removal decisions appear arbitrary. FDA questions why analyte X was removed but analyte Y (with similar weak performance) was kept. Concerns about bias or data manipulation. Submission requests for additional analytical work on removed analytes (1–3 month delay). Investors question governance rigor.
  • No pre-registration of clinical studies: without ClinicalTrials.gov registration before enrollment, the company can be accused of 'p-hacking' (cherry-picking endpoints and analysis plans after data collection to show favorable results). FDA and payers view unregistered studies with skepticism, discounting the evidence. Clinical adoption slowed by 12–24 months; payer coverage denied. Reputational damage comparable to selective-reporting scandals in other fields.
  • Vague or unenforced marketing guardrails: if the company or its investors claim '500 tests per drop' in pitch decks or press releases before clusters are validated, FDA may view it as over-claiming, and clinicians/payers may become skeptical if real results show fewer validated analytes at launch. Regulatory warning or consent agreement delaying clearance (2–4 months). Adoption slowed by 12–24 months. Investor loss of confidence if over-promise creates credibility deficit.
  • Poorly designed or static Analyte Removal Log: if removals are documented in internal spreadsheets but not published, or if the company documents failures in vague terms ('redesign ongoing') without root cause, the log adds no credibility. Worse, if a board member or FDA inspector discovers internal notes contradicting the public transparency report, trust collapses. Remediation: acknowledgment of failure to disclose, potential regulatory action, valuation impact 20–40% (estimated).
  • Absence of Scientific Advisory Board authority: if the board is advisory-only with no veto or recusal power, and the company publishes results the board disagrees with, the board loses credibility. Board members may resign publicly or refuse to endorse the company's submissions. Loss of external credibility: Series B and payer confidence impaired. Conversely, if the board has veto power over publications, it may suppress or delay valid science, damaging credibility with academics and clinicians.
  • Inadequate conflict-of-interest disclosures: if a board member fails to disclose a competing commercial interest (e.g., also advising a rival diagnostics company), and this is discovered during due diligence, the entire board's independence is questioned. Investor and regulator trust damaged. The company may need to reconstitute the board (3–4 month delay).
  • Late or missing publication of quarterly transparency reports: if quarterly reports are delayed beyond Month 6 (2027-04-13) or content is incomplete, investors and stakeholders assume data is being withheld. Rumors and media speculation fill the gap. Series B due diligence stalls. Regulatory review asks pointed questions about data quality. Impact: 2–3 month delay in fundraising or regulatory milestone.

Worst Case Scenario: The company publishes optimistic pre-launch communications claiming the 500-test vision without scientific backing, attracting Series A investment and market hype. By Month 12 (2027-10-13), analytical feasibility studies reveal 30–50% of proposed analytes cannot meet accuracy or cross-reactivity thresholds. Internal team debates whether to disclose failures or quietly remove analytes. No public transparency plan is in place. The company delays disclosure by 2–3 months while redesign attempts fail. A departing employee or competitor leaks evidence of suppressed failures to media. FDA learns of discrepancies during Pre-Submission and questions whether the company can be trusted with future submissions. Investors discover the hidden failures during Series B diligence and withdraw or demand severe terms (30–50% discount, founder equity dilution). Clinicians and payers, reading leaked news, view the product as oversold and delay adoption. The company's credibility is destroyed before the product reaches market; valuation collapses 50–80%; Series B is blocked or proceeds only with replacement of management; launch is delayed 12–24 months or product is abandoned. Total impact: USD 15–30 million in value destruction, 18–36 month timeline extension or product failure.

Best Case Scenario: The company adopts the Science-First Transparency Charter at Month 1 (2026-11-13), recruits a credible 5-member Scientific Advisory Board with published track records in diagnostics and assay chemistry, and launches a public Analyte Performance Dashboard by Month 3 (2027-01-13). As Cluster 1 analytes are developed over Months 3–12 (2027-01-13 to 2027-10-13), the monthly dashboard shows each analyte's progress transparently: which pass thresholds, which are in redesign, and which fail and are removed. Failure causes are documented with technical detail (e.g., 'cross-reactivity with endogenous interferent X at 8× physiologic level; attempted redesign with alternative antibody; still failed; removed Month 9 = 2027-07-13'). By Month 6 (2027-04-13), the first quarterly transparency report is published showing 12 of 15 planned analytes passing thresholds, 2 in redesign, 1 removed; FDA and investors see a rigorous, disciplined program. Series A investors gain confidence that the team is honest about challenges. By Month 12 (2027-10-13), Cluster 1 is locked at 12 validated analytes; the dashboard and published transparency reports have established the company as transparent and trustworthy. FDA Pre-Submission feedback, informed by the published data, confirms the regulatory pathway. Clinical-study enrollment proceeds with high recruitment because clinicians see the company is publishing results openly. By Month 18 (2028-04-13), clinical concordance is published peer-reviewed, showing ≥95% agreement on Cluster 1 analytes with reference methods. Payers and clinicians cite the published data as evidence of rigor. Series B closes at favorable terms (no steep discount) because investors view the company as a credible, evidence-driven, de-risked opportunity. Regulatory review of the 510(k) is smooth because the company's quality system, study design, and claims are well-aligned with published evidence. Product launch succeeds with faster clinician adoption and payer coverage because the reputation for transparency is established. Cumulative impact: 6–12 month timeline acceleration on Series B and regulatory review; reduced reputational risk; competitive differentiation as 'the transparent diagnostics company'; higher Series B valuation (+15–25% estimated).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage an independent clinical research organization (CRO) or academic medical center as a co-author and co-owner of clinical-study data and publications, rather than having the company own and publish unilaterally. The CRO/academic partner publishes independently, reducing perceived bias and increasing credibility. Cost: USD 500k–1M in study-design and data-sharing fees. Timeline: Same (studies still pre-registered and published, but co-authored). Benefit: external authorship eliminates appearance of company cherry-picking; regulatory and investor confidence higher. Trade-off: company cedes some control over publication timing and framing.
  • Establish a 'public data repository' (e.g., hosted on Zenodo, Figshare, or a company-maintained site with immutable version control) where all raw assay results, analyte-removal documentation, and monthly dashboard snapshots are published under a Creative Commons license, allowing external researchers to audit and re-analyze. Company publishes monthly summaries and quarterly reports; researchers can access underlying data if they sign a data-use agreement. Cost: USD 20–50k for infrastructure and legal review. Benefit: extreme transparency and external audit capability, differentiates the company as 'most transparent,' creates research partnerships. Trade-off: raises risk of competitors or hostile actors using data against the company; company must be comfortable with high-resolution data disclosure.
  • Establish a 'Real-World Evidence Program' in parallel to clinical studies: once Cluster 1 is commercially cleared (Months 36–48 = 2029-10-13 to 2030-10-13), enroll 1,000+ patients in a long-term registry collecting anonymized results. Publish quarterly registry updates (e.g., 'Cluster 1 analyte performance in 1,000-patient real-world cohort'), showing how accuracy and clinical utility hold up outside the controlled study setting. Cost: USD 500k–2M over 3 years. Benefit: generates rich real-world evidence for payer coverage and further Clusters; transparency extends to post-market monitoring. Trade-off: ongoing cost and legal/privacy complexity; depends on product being on market first.
  • Partner with a leading medical journal (e.g., JAMA, Lancet) as a 'strategic publishing partner,' committing to publish major results and analyte-removal data in that journal quarterly or semi-annually, with guaranteed rapid review and publication. Journal gains high-impact content; company gains third-party editorial rigor and visibility. Cost: journal may request fee-per-article (USD 5–10k) or agree to no fee if impact is high. Benefit: journal's editorial oversight increases credibility; publication in high-impact venue reaches clinicians and regulators. Trade-off: journal controls final messaging; company must cede editorial control.
  • Commission an independent third-party 'Science Auditor' (e.g., retired FDA scientist, academic pathology professor) to audit the company's assay performance and removal decisions quarterly, and publish an independent audit report. Auditor reports to board and stakeholders (not company). Cost: USD 100–200k per year for quarterly audits. Benefit: external, independent authority validates rigor; differentiates company as 'externally audited.' Trade-off: company must accept potential critical findings and commit to transparency even if unfavorable.
  • If the Scientific Advisory Board approach is under-resourced or recruitment is slow, establish a 'Virtual Advisory Board' using asynchronous online participation (Slack, email, quarterly video calls) rather than quarterly in-person meetings. Lowers cost of recruitment and retention. Board reviews and comments on monthly dashboard and quarterly reports within 2 weeks. Requirement: email or video sign-off from ≥3 of 5 board members before reports are published. Cost: USD 50–75k/year (vs. USD 100–150k for in-person meetings). Benefit: faster recruitment, lower overhead. Trade-off: less cohesion and relationship-building; may feel less credible to external stakeholders.
  • If pre-registration on ClinicalTrials.gov is delayed, use a free pre-registration service like the Open Science Framework (OSF), AsPredicted, or Protocols.io to register the clinical-study protocol before enrollment. OSF and AsPredicted allow time-stamped, immutable registration and are acceptable to many journals and FDA. Cost: USD 0–5k. Timeline: same. Benefit: satisfies pre-registration requirement and some regulators without ClinicalTrials.gov; faster if NIH registration is delayed. Trade-off: less visibility than ClinicalTrials.gov; some payers and regulators may not recognize these platforms.
  • If development is fast and analytes are ready for commercial release before the full Scientific Advisory Board is in place or the quarterly reporting schedule is active, 'fast-track' the transparency program: (1) retrospectively compile a 'Science-First Accountability Statement' summarizing which analytes were validated, which failed, and removal rationales, within 30 days of the first commercial sale; (2) commit to prospective quarterly reports and a functioning advisory board within 90 days of launch. Cost: USD 50–100k for historical documentation. Benefit: product can launch while transparency infrastructure is being built. Trade-off: appears reactive rather than proactive; regulators and early customers may view it as incomplete.

Create Document 10: Fallback Product V1 Definition and Scope-Retreat Protocol

ID: c195556d-03ff-48bf-9b70-076438b37c47

Description: Pre-registered Fallback Panel V1: 50-analyte core menu (approximately 4-5 cartridges of 10-15 analytes each), selected for high clinical value, low cross-reactivity risk, established reference methods. Specifies automatic activation trigger: if any Month 12 or 18 (2027-10-13 or 2028-04-13) gate is failed and unresolved by Month 15 (2028-01-13), board votes within 5 business days to activate Fallback V1 without further negotiation. Includes staffing contingency (-20-30% headcount reduction), Newark Phase 2 pause, Clusters 2-5 development pause, and revised timeline to clearance. Documents that fallback is a technical pivot, not a failure, and ensures the company ships a validated product instead of abandoning development. Primary audience: board, investors, team. Prevents sunk-cost escalation and company failure.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer

Primary Template: Product scope and retreat decision tree; contingency planning template

Secondary Template: Staffing reduction and redeployment plan; revised timeline and budget for fallback product

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 1 (2026-11-13), define Fallback V1 scope: 50 highest-clinical-value analytes, 4-5 cartridges, cumulative menu messaging, same manufacturing/regulatory approach but narrower breadth.
  • Document activation trigger: if Month 12 (2027-10-13) yield <80% (mean, or lower CI <75%), or Month 18 (2028-04-13) shelf-life <9 months or clinical concordance <93%, and 4-week design review does not resolve by Month 15 (2028-01-13), activate fallback.
  • Specify board voting procedure: CEO presents fallback-activation motion within 2 weeks of gate failure; majority board vote required; execution within 5 business days (pause Newark Phase 2 spend, notify contractors, activate staffing reduction plan).
  • Include fallback staffing plan: reduce headcount by 20-30% (pause research hires, consolidate teams), pause Clusters 2-5 work, reprioritize toward Fallback V1 validation and regulatory submission.
  • Document fallback timeline to clearance: estimated 6-9 months additional (50-analyte menu has lower validation burden than full 500-test roadmap).
  • Establish fallback budget: Series A total covers USD 12-15M burn for Fallback V1 path; no Series B needed before clearance if gates delay <6 months.
  • Communicate fallback strategy to investors before Series A close: frame as risk-management, not weakness.

Approval Authorities: Board of Directors, CEO, Chief Financial Officer

Essential Information:

  • Define the Fallback Panel V1 scope: exactly which 50 analytes are selected, and the clinical justification for each (high-value outcomes, established reference methods, low cross-reactivity risk, feasibility at <USD 25/cartridge COGS).
  • Specify the automatic retreat trigger: quantitative gate thresholds (yield, concordance, shelf-life, lot CV) at which Fallback V1 activation is mandatory, independent of timeline or schedule pressure.
  • Document the board voting procedure: who votes, quorum, timeline from gate failure to fallback decision (proposed: 2-week presentation window, 5-day execution deadline).
  • Detail staffing and redeployment plan: headcount reduction magnitude, which roles/teams are paused (Clusters 2-5 R&D, non-essential Newark spend), and which are redeployed to Fallback V1.
  • Establish fallback timeline and budget: revised clearance date for 50-analyte panel (estimated 6-9 months shorter than full 500-test roadmap), total cumulative burn to clearance, and confirmation that Series A funding covers this path without Series B before clearance.
  • Specify fallback regulatory strategy: does Fallback V1 use the same 510(k) pathway planned for Cluster 1, or is a simpler clearance route available (fewer analytes may reduce evidence burden).
  • Articulate fallback market positioning: how 50-analyte menu is marketed and priced differently from the 500-test vision (cumulative menu claim paused; 'comprehensive core panel' messaging).
  • Include success criteria for Fallback V1: what must be true (concordance ≥95%, shelf-life ≥12 months, yield ≥85%) for fallback to proceed, and what constitutes success post-launch (adoption, reimbursement, revenue ramp).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Unclear retreat trigger allows sunk-cost escalation: if gate failures are met with design-review extensions rather than fallback activation, USD 2–10 million (estimate) in Newark and clinical spend continues without evidence of feasibility, draining capital and extending timeline to resolution by 6–12 months.
  • Ambiguous board voting procedure delays the fallback decision by 4–8 weeks while leadership debates interpretation of gate results, allowing momentum and denial to override quantitative thresholds; each week of delay costs USD 100–300k in burn (estimate).
  • Staffing redeployment plan absent causes layoff chaos: without clear criteria for which roles are retained/paused, HR and team morale suffer, key people leave, and critical Fallback V1 work is understaffed; estimated 20–30% turnover and 2–4 month productivity loss.
  • Fallback timeline overly optimistic (e.g., 'same as Cluster 1') misleads investors about Series A coverage; if actual fallback-to-clearance timeline is 12 months longer than planned, Series B is required months earlier than budgeted, forcing emergency fundraising at disadvantageous valuation.
  • Fallback regulatory pathway undefined means clinical studies, FDA submissions and quality documentation designed for 500 analytes cannot be repurposed for 50; last-minute re-engineering of study design costs USD 500k–1M and adds 3–6 months (estimate).
  • Fallback market positioning not pre-planned risks credibility loss: if the company pivots to 50 analytes and positions it as 'narrower' rather than 'core validated,' payers and clinicians perceive it as a failed product and adoption stalls; estimated 6–12 month market delay.

Worst Case Scenario: Without a pre-agreed Fallback Product V1 and clear retreat triggers, the company misses an analytical feasibility gate at Month 12 (2027-10-13)—e.g., cross-reactivity limits effective panel to ~150 analytes, yield falls to 70%, or shelf-life is only 6 months. Leadership initiates a '4-week design review,' extends the gate decision to Month 15 (2028-01-13), invests an additional USD 1–2 million in redesign and re-testing, and by Month 18 (2028-04-13) still cannot resolve the root issue. At this point, Newark Phase 2 capital (USD 2–3 million) is already committed or spent, clinical studies are enrolled but underpowered for the revised analyte set, and the company has USD 10–15 million in sunk costs. A forced pivot to a 50-analyte fallback at Month 18 (2028-04-13) requires re-designing clinical studies, re-submitting to FDA, and re-negotiating payer coverage—adding 6–12 months and USD 1–2 million to timeline and cost. Series A capital is exhausted before clearance, forcing a dilutive down-round or bridge financing at 40–60% discount (10–20% equity loss estimated). The company loses investor and team confidence, experiences 30–50% turnover among senior staff, and either shuts down or merges at a significant valuation discount (50–80% haircut estimated).

Best Case Scenario: With a pre-registered Fallback Panel V1 and quantitative retreat triggers, analytical results at Month 12 (2027-10-13) show yield ≥85%, concordance ≥95%, and shelf-life ≥12 months across all Cluster 1 analytes. The lead cluster passes the gate and proceeds to clinical studies and FDA submission on schedule. If later gate (Month 18 = 2028-04-13) reveals cross-reactivity or sensitivity issues in 20% of analytes, the company identifies failures by Month 12 (2027-10-13) and uses the 4-week design review to remove problematic analytes and strengthen the remaining set. By Month 18 (2028-04-13), design is frozen with a narrower but more robust cluster; fallback activation is not needed. If an unlikely scenario requires fallback (e.g., mid-clinical unanticipated stability drift), the board votes within 2 weeks at Month 15 (2028-01-13), staffing is redeployed in the following week, and the 50-analyte Fallback V1 proceeds to FDA submission at Month 36 (2029-10-13) with high confidence. Series A capital covers both paths; Series B is not needed before clearance. The company ships a validated product by Month 48 (2030-10-13), gains payer coverage and clinical adoption with no credibility loss (transparent gate process and pre-announced fallback build trust), and launches with a clear path to expanding the menu post-clearance. Investors view the disciplined gate process as a risk-management strength, Series B is oversubscribed, and the company reaches profitability by Year 4–5 post-launch.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If defining Fallback V1 scope at Month 1 (2026-11-13) is too early due to incomplete analyte data, schedule a 4-week analyte-assessment sprint (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-13 to 2026-11-13) using literature, reference-lab data, and industry benchmarks to pre-select the top 50 high-value analytes, then lock Fallback V1 scope as a binding definition by Month 2 (2026-12-13).
  • If board voting procedure is contentious or time-consuming, establish a standing 'Feasibility Committee' (3–5 board/investor members) with pre-delegated authority to vote on fallback activation within 5 business days of the CEO's motion; full board approves the decision in the next regular meeting (informational, not re-vote) to preserve momentum.
  • If headcount reduction triggers layoffs and legal complexity, pre-arrange a workforce flexibility plan by Month 6 (2027-04-13): designate contractor or part-time roles (e.g., clinical monitoring, regulatory writing) that can be scaled down without severance; rotate core staff to 80–90% FTE if burn reduction is needed, preserving intellectual property continuity.
  • If fallback timeline uncertainty creates Series A anxiety, develop two detailed roadmaps (Cluster 1 and Fallback V1) with identical regulatory and manufacturing steps, so that fallback activation at Month 18 (2028-04-13) does not change the pathway—only the analyte roster. Series A board material includes both timelines from the start; investors know fallback clearance is Month 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13) and Series A USD 12–15M (estimate) covers both.
  • If the 50-analyte Fallback V1 scope cannot achieve the proposed USD 25/cartridge COGS ceiling due to economies of scale lost, reduce fallback to a 30–35 analyte 'essential core' at USD 15–18/cartridge, ensuring gross margin ≥60% even at lower per-run revenue (USD 75–100) and full market credibility. This variant still provides a defensible, profitable product.
  • If fallback market positioning risks brand damage (perception of 'narrowed vision'), rebrand fallback as 'Tier 1' validated core (50 analytes) with a public roadmap to 'Tier 2' (expansion clusters) post-launch, positioning it as a phased-expansion strategy rather than a retreat. Market the core with confidence and announce Cluster 2 development in parallel to retain the 500-test narrative long-term.

Create Document 11: Pharma Beachhead and Non-Dilutive Funding Strategy

ID: 15922057-6766-412d-b223-3b637ea7d1ab

Description: Strategy to generate revenue and validation data from pharma sponsors and grants, reducing equity-dilution pressure and funding-runway risk. Targets 2-3 feasibility partnerships with pharma customers by Month 6 (2027-04-13) (unfunded), first paid contract (USD 50-100k for 1,000 samples) by Month 9 (2027-07-13), and cumulative USD 1-2M in pharma contracts + grants by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Specifies SBIR/STTR Phase I applications (USD 150-200k each, targeting NIH, NSF, DOE), grant-application timeline, pharma contract negotiation approach (biomarker monitoring, drug-development studies), and lean-pivot trigger (if run-rate stays below USD 100k/month by Month 18 = 2028-04-13, reduce headcount and pause Phase 2 Newark). Primary audience: CEO, CFO, commercial lead. Validates market demand early and de-risks funding.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Executive Officer and Chief Product Officer (with business-development support)

Primary Template: SBIR/STTR grant application template; pharma partnership agreement template

Secondary Template: Revenue recognition policy; pharma customer agreement and IP provisions

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 0 (2026-10-13), identify 5-10 pharma companies or CROs with biomarker-monitoring or drug-development partnerships; initiate conversations.
  • By Month 3 (2027-01-13), launch SBIR Phase I applications (USD 150-200k each); target 2-3 grants. Expected award timeline: Months 10-12 (2027-08-13 to 2027-10-13).
  • By Month 6 (2027-04-13), have 2-3 pharma feasibility partnerships in place (unfunded, data-sharing for proof-of-concept).
  • By Month 9 (2027-07-13), negotiate first paid pharma contract: scope (1,000-5,000 patient samples), contract value (USD 50-100k), timeline (Months 10-15 = 2027-08-13 to 2028-01-13), IP/publication terms.
  • By Month 12 (2027-10-13), secure cumulative commitments: USD 500k-1M SBIR/STTR + USD 500k-1M pharma = USD 1-2M total.
  • Establish lean-pivot trigger: if pharma/grant run-rate stays below USD 100k/month at Month 18 (2028-04-13), reduce headcount 20-30%, pause full Newark Phase 2 build, and shift to contract-manufacturing model.
  • Track pharma pipeline monthly; update board quarterly on revenue trajectory and pivot-trigger status.

Approval Authorities: Chief Executive Officer, Chief Product Officer, Board of Directors

Essential Information:

  • Define the explicit pharma-partner identification and outreach strategy: which therapeutic areas, company types (pharma, CRO, biotech), and decision-makers to target by Month 0 (2026-10-13); list target organizations and their biomarker-monitoring priorities.
  • Specify SBIR/STTR application calendar: which agencies (NIH, NSF, DOE) to target, application submission dates (Months 2–3 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-01-13), expected funding amounts per agency, and awards timeline (Months 10–12 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-10-13).
  • Detail the pharma contract-negotiation approach: typical contract structure (scope, sample count, payment terms), payment schedule (upfront, milestone, or ramp), IP and publication rights, and typical pharma decision timeline (6–12 months from initial conversation to signed contract).
  • Quantify the pharma revenue trajectory: feasibility partnerships (unfunded) Months 0–6 (2026-10-13 to 2027-04-13), first paid contract (USD 50–100 k, Months 10–15 = 2027-08-13 to 2028-01-13), and cumulative commitments USD 1–2 M by Month 12 (2027-10-13); specify monthly run-rate projections Months 12–24 (2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13).
  • Define the lean-pivot trigger operational plan: what constitutes 'below USD 100 k/month' (cumulative pharma + grant income?), which cost-cutting actions occur first (staff reduction headcount %? pausing which programs?), and trigger decision authority (who votes, timeline for pivot activation).
  • Establish risk mitigations specific to pharma partnerships: typical delays (timeline buffer for negotiation extension), pharma financial insolvency or program cancellation (probability and impact), and contingency (which targets to activate if primary contract falls through, time to activate backup USD 50–100 k contract).
  • Specify grant-application and award-management logistics: which SBIR/STTR program phase and track; pre-award due diligence (IP review, eligibility confirmation); post-award compliance (reporting, milestone tracking); and effort allocation (who leads applications, estimated cost of preparation and compliance USD 20–40 k).
  • Detail the revenue-recognition and accounting treatment: how pharma payments are classified (R&D contract revenue vs. grant revenue vs. equity dilution offset); cash-collection risk (typical accounts-receivable days for pharma, milestone holdbacks); and monthly tracking for the lean-pivot trigger.
  • Quantify the marketing and business-development effort: headcount (business-development lead by Month 1 = 2026-11-13? = 2026-11-13); travel and conferencing budget (pharma industry events, CRO meetings); relationship-building timeline to first contract (estimate 6–9 months from initial introduction to signed contract); and monthly activity targets (calls, meetings, RFP responses).
  • Define success metrics and reporting cadence: monthly pharma-pipeline reports (stage of negotiation, expected close date, contract value); quarterly board updates on revenue trajectory vs. lean-pivot trigger; and leading indicators (number of feasibility partnerships, proposals submitted, LOIs received) by Month 6 (2027-04-13).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Pharma partners are not identified or engaged by Month 0 (2026-10-13), delaying first feasibility partnership from Month 6 (2027-04-13) to Month 9–12 (2027-07-13 to 2027-10-13); this cascades into first paid contract at Month 12–15 (2027-10-13 to 2028-01-13) instead of Month 9 (2027-07-13), reducing non-dilutive income by USD 500 k–1 M and increasing Series A funding pressure by 30–50%.
  • SBIR/STTR grant applications are not submitted by Month 3 (2027-01-13) deadline or are submitted without sufficient preliminary data, resulting in no awards or delayed awards beyond Month 12 (2027-10-13); this forgoes USD 300–500 k in non-dilutive funding and increases Series A dilution by 3–5%.
  • Pharma contract terms are not pre-negotiated (e.g., IP ownership, publication rights, payment terms), causing legal disputes or delays post-signature; ambiguity on IP rights can block internal publication and credibility-building, costing 2–4 months and USD 50–100 k in legal fees.
  • Lean-pivot trigger is not defined quantitatively, so a USD 75 k/month run-rate at Month 18 (2028-04-13) does not trigger pivot decision, causing continued high burn and funding shortfall; lack of clarity leads to 4–8 week decision delay and USD 200–400 k in avoidable spending.
  • Pharma revenue projections are not tracked monthly, so the company discovers at Month 18 (2028-04-13) that cumulative income is only USD 200 k instead of USD 500 k–1 M; untracked pipeline leaves Series A investors unaware of deteriorating funding outlook until emergency bridge round is needed.
  • Grant-application logistics and compliance are not planned, resulting in missed reporting deadlines, loss of funds, or grant clawback; estimates for award complexity and effort are underestimated, consuming 2–4 FTE-months of unbudgeted work.
  • Pharma contracts are structured as single large blocks (e.g., USD 500 k in one contract) rather than staggered payments, creating cash-flow lumpy-ness and risk if the contract is cancelled or delayed; loss of a single contract represents 50%+ of budgeted non-dilutive income.
  • Business-development headcount is not hired (no business lead by Month 1 = 2026-11-13), leaving pharma outreach to the CEO or technical team; executive distraction and slow relationship-building delay first contract by 6–12 months and reduce quality of partnerships.

Worst Case Scenario: No pharma partners are secured and no SBIR/STTR awards are received by Month 12 (2027-10-13); the company discovers at Month 12 (2027-10-13) that the USD 1–2 M non-dilutive funding assumption is zero and Series A is insufficient to cover burn through Month 24 (2028-10-13). Emergency bridge financing at a 40–60% valuation discount is required, diluting founders by an additional 10–15% and raising cumulative dilution by Month 24 (2028-10-13) to 35–45%. Alternatively, the company is forced to pause development, lay off 40–50% of staff (including early hires), and delay design freeze from Month 18 (2028-04-13) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13), pushing FDA submission and clinical launch by 6–12 months. The credibility loss from public layoffs, combined with delayed clinical evidence, reduces Series B funding likelihood by 30–50% and delays profitability by 18–24 months.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 12 (2027-10-13), the company has signed 2–3 pharma feasibility partnerships (unfunded) and closed two paid pharma contracts totaling USD 300–500 k, with monthly run-rate of USD 50–100 k. SBIR Phase I awards total USD 300–400 k received or committed. Cumulative non-dilutive income reaches USD 600 k–900 k, reducing Series A dilution need by USD 600 k–900 k and extending runway by 2–3 months without additional equity raise. Monthly pharma and grant income covers 20–30% of Month 12–18 (2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) burn, reducing equity dilution from Series A2 and Series A3 by 15–25%. Board has confidence in revenue pathway and approves full Newark Phase 2 capital release at Month 18 (2028-04-13). Pharma partnerships also provide real-world sample access for clinical validation studies, accelerating analytical feasibility gates and reducing clinical-study recruitment risk. First commercial sales cycle is enabled by published pharma partnership results and demonstrated payer/clinician interest.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If pharma partnerships are difficult to secure by Month 6 (2027-04-13), activate a narrower beachhead: instead of 'biomarker monitoring in drug development' (broad), target one high-value disease area (e.g., rare genetic metabolic disorder, cancer immunotherapy) with 2–3 identified sponsors already known to have unmet biomarker needs; cost: USD 30–50 k in market research and 2–3 executive relationship-building trips by Month 3 (2027-01-13).
  • If SBIR/STTR grant awards are delayed beyond Month 12 (2027-10-13), pursue venture debt from alternative lenders (Silicon Valley Bank, Gold Hill Capital, etc.) in USD 500 k–1 M tranches as a bridge to Series A; cost: 2–4% annual interest + 1% fees, with 3–5 year repayment; this defers equity dilution but increases debt service burden post-launch.
  • If pharma contract value is lower than expected (USD 20–50 k instead of USD 50–100 k), expand the number of smaller contracts (target 5–10 contracts of USD 20–30 k each instead of 2–3 large contracts); this increases business-development effort by 2–3× but diversifies revenue risk and may provide 3–6 month earlier revenue ramp.
  • If the lean-pivot trigger is hit at Month 18 (2028-04-13) (pharma run-rate below USD 100 k/month), activate a contract-research-organization (CRO) partnership instead of full in-house manufacturing: outsource all filling, assembly and packaging to an established CRO (e.g., NAMSA, Eurofins) for clinical-scale volumes; reduces Newark capital commitment from USD 2–3 M to USD 500–800 k and defers manufacturing headcount; cost: USD 50–100 per cartridge (vs USD 25 internal target), reducing gross margin by 15–25%, but extends runway by 6–9 months without additional equity raise.
  • If pharma partnerships stall due to IP or publication disputes, establish a separate subsidiary or joint venture (JV) for pharma-sponsored research that is operationally isolated from the core product company; IP and publication are governed by JV agreements, protecting core product IP while enabling pharma collaboration; cost: USD 20–30 k legal setup and ongoing compliance; timeline: 4–6 weeks to negotiate JV terms.
  • If business-development headcount cannot be hired at market rates (USD 150–200 k) due to budget constraints, engage a fractional commercial advisor or consultant (0.5–1.0 FTE equivalent, USD 80–120 k/year) by Month 1 (2026-11-13) to lead pharma outreach; cost is lower, but continuity and relationship-depth may suffer; mitigate by requiring the consultant to transfer relationships to an internal hire by Month 9 (2027-07-13).
  • If the company discovers that SBIR/STTR eligibility is unclear (e.g., if a founder has prior SBIR awards or the company has excess venture funding), engage a grants-compliance consultant (USD 5–10 k) to verify eligibility and optimize applications; this avoids costly application rejections and ensures maximum award amounts.

Create Document 12: Risk Register and Mitigation Plan (Enterprise Risk Management)

ID: a075507b-1108-4f0b-b0d1-d873fec231f0

Description: Comprehensive risk register documenting 25+ identified risks (analytical infeasibility, regulatory uncertainty, funding gap, unit economics, reputational, supply-chain, clinical-study delays, software/cybersecurity, competitive response, etc.) with likelihood, severity, mitigation actions, owners, and review cadence. Organized by category (technical, regulatory, financial, operational, market, reputational). Includes contingency triggers (e.g., yield <80% at Month 12 = 2027-10-13 activates fallback; De Novo confirmed at Month 6 = 2027-04-13 activates Series B contingency funding). Monthly risk review with leadership team; board briefing quarterly. Primary audience: leadership, board, investors. Prevents surprise escalations and ensures early contingency activation.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Executive Officer (with Chief Risk Officer or equivalent cross-functional risk owner)

Primary Template: ISO 31000 risk management framework; project risk register template

Secondary Template: Contingency planning and escalation protocol

Steps to Create:

  • Document all 25 identified risks with likelihood (High/Medium/Low), severity (High/Medium/Low), and current mitigation status.
  • For each risk, specify: owner (responsible person), mitigation action, success metric, review cadence, escalation trigger.
  • Group risks by category: analytical feasibility, regulatory pathway, funding, unit economics, reputational, supply-chain, clinical validation, software, talent, competitive.
  • Establish risk-review meeting cadence: monthly with leadership (CTO, quality, operations, CFO, commercial); quarterly board briefing.
  • Define contingency activation rules: if risk likelihood becomes 'High' or if mitigation fails, activate pre-planned contingency (e.g., fallback product, bridge financing, CLIA parallel route).
  • Track contingency status: track which contingencies are pre-positioned, funded, and ready to activate within <2 weeks.
  • Update register monthly; refresh at each gate (Months 6, 12, 18 = 2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13).

Approval Authorities: Chief Executive Officer, Board of Directors

Essential Information:

  • Document the 25+ identified risks from assumptions.md and project-plan.md, organized by category: analytical feasibility, regulatory pathway, funding, unit economics, reputational, supply-chain, clinical validation, software/cybersecurity, talent acquisition, and competitive.
  • For each risk, specify: risk ID, name, description, likelihood (High/Medium/Low), severity (High/Medium/Low), root cause, current status of mitigation, and mitigation action owner.
  • Define contingency activation rules: specify the trigger condition (e.g., 'yield <80% at Month 12 = 2027-10-13'), the decision threshold (e.g., 'lower 95% confidence interval <75%'), and the pre-planned contingency (e.g., 'retreat to Fallback V1').
  • Establish risk-review cadence: monthly leadership review (CTO, quality, operations, CFO, commercial); quarterly board briefing; annual strategy refresh.
  • Track contingency pre-positioning: specify which contingencies are funded, approved, and ready to activate within <2 weeks (e.g., CLIA lab fallback, Series B emergency timeline, bridge financing), and document their status.
  • Develop escalation protocol: define which risks trigger automatic executive decision (e.g., yield miss, regulatory surprise) versus which require board vote, and establish decision timeline (<1 week for operational escalations, <2 weeks for capital decisions).
  • Create a risk heat map by likelihood × severity; identify top 5-10 risks requiring active monitoring and contingency pre-positioning.
  • Specify success metrics for each mitigation: e.g., 'Dual suppliers qualified by Month 6 (2027-04-13) with signed quality agreements' or 'Pre-Submission held by Month 6 (2027-04-13) with written FDA feedback on regulatory pathway'.
  • Link risks to gates: identify which risks gate release of capital (e.g., analytical feasibility gates Month 6, 12, 18 = 2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13) and which are continuous-monitoring risks.
